If the Congress, within twenty-one days after receipt of the latter written declaration, or, if Congress is not in session, within twenty-one days after Congress is required to assemble, determines by two-thirds vote of both Houses that the President is unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office, the Vice President shall continue to discharge the same as Acting President; otherwise, the President shall resume the powers and duties of his office.

—

Amendment XXVI: Voting Age Lowered to 18

Section 1: Lowering of Voting Age to 18

Section 1. The right of citizens of the United States, who are eighteen years of age or older, to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of age.

Section 2: Enforcement Clause

Section 2. The Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation.

—

Amendment XXVII: Congressional Pay Change Delays

No law, varying the compensation for the services of the Senators and Representatives, shall take effect, until an election of Representatives shall have intervened.

More to come later, including the table describing the amendments to the United States Constitution to be added soon.

item.title: Labor Stoppage Amendment (LSA)
item.dc:creator: allenacnguyen
item.content:encoded:
I, Allen Nguyen — an independent citizen from Houston, TX, and a Summa Cum Laude graduate from the University of Houston with a Bachelor of Science in Digital Media degree — introduce a constitutional amendment that would allow public sector workers (employees) the right to strike or organize work stoppages, and the employers' right to impose lockouts, without facing penalties like forfeiture of pension and re-employment rights by the state government.

Amendment Slogan

"Protect the Workers. Preserve the Rights."

Update 7/5/2026: Updated font format on Exhibits and Structural Continuity sections.

Labor Stoppage Amendment

Section 1: The Right to Work Stoppage

Section 1.

1–1: Employee Right to Work Stoppage. The right of employees in both the public and private sectors to engage in strikes, work stoppages, or other collective labor actions in connection with labor disputes — including disputes over compensation, insurance, benefits, staffing levels, workplace safety, and terms or conditions of employment — shall not be denied, abridged, or infringed by the United States or any State.

1–2: Employer Right to Lockout, Limitations on Lockouts, and Private Sector Insolvency Exemption. Employers and their designated executives in both the public and private sectors shall retain the right to impose lockouts during labor disputes; provided that such lockouts do not exceed a cumulative total of fourteen calendar days per dispute, do not result in the permanent replacement or termination of employees, do not disrupt essential or critical services as defined or regulated under Sections 3 and 4, and do not infringe upon the benefit and seniority protections guaranteed herein. On the fifteenth calendar day of an active lockout, or upon any lockout enacted in bad faith to deplete union resources without active collective bargaining, such action shall be explicitly deemed an unlawful economic penalty and a constructive termination. This milestone shall trigger immediate full backpay liabilities for the employer and the instant suspension of all employee non-compete covenants for the remaining duration of the dispute; except that in the private sector, an employer may petition a court of competent jurisdiction for a temporary extension of a lockout solely upon a clear and convincing showing of extreme operational insolvency that threatens the permanent cessation of all business operations; provided that such insolvency must be demonstrated across the consolidated financial structure of the employer's entire corporate enterprise, including all parent companies, domestic or international subsidiaries, holding companies, and controlled affiliates.

1–3: Non-Forfeiture of Accrued Vested Benefits and Anti-Retaliation Protection. No person shall suffer the forfeiture, reduction, suspension, or adverse recalculation of pension or retirement benefits, nor the suspension, termination, or reduction of employer contributions toward health, life, disability, or other welfare insurance plans, nor any loss of accrued seniority, service-credit hours, re-employment rights, or any other penalty or retaliation for participating in such labor actions. All retirement benefits and credits accrued prior to or during a protected labor action shall be deemed unalterable, vested property of the employee. No employee shall be permanently replaced, terminated, subjected to economic layoff, or otherwise economically penalized for participating in a protected labor action.

1–4: Prohibitions on Labor Substitutions, Military Interventions, and Algorithmic Strikebreaking

Subsection 1–4(a): Prohibition on Human Personnel Substitution. During a protected labor action or any period where work is withheld due to a failure of timely compensation, no employer, nor any official of the United States or any State, shall temporarily or permanently replace, substitute, or supplement the striking personnel to perform the operational, specialized, security, management, or administrative functions historically performed by the affected bargaining unit.

Subsection 1–4(b): Restrictions on External Workforces, Funding Status, and National Guard Deployment. The prohibition established in subsection (a) shall explicitly apply to the deployment of personnel from other agencies, departments, sub-agencies, or external workforces; private third-party independent contractors; temporary staffing agencies; or any corporate parent, subsidiary, or affiliated division. No officer of the United States, any State, or any political subdivision thereof shall evade the protections of this article through the temporary reassignment, detail, deputization, cross-designation, emergency designation, or interagency transfer of personnel to perform duties historically performed by the affected bargaining unit. This prohibition further bars any internal non-bargaining unit employees, salaried managers, corporate executives, or workers from unaffected internal divisions performing functions outside their historical daily duties — as well as the emergency deployment, or increased operational utilization and scaling, of automated systems, generative software, and artificial intelligence designed to mimic or replace human labor functions historically performed by the bargaining unit. The National Guard and military reserves may be deployed to perform bargaining unit functions solely and exclusively upon a binding judicial declaration that such deployment is the single available means to avert an instantaneous, catastrophic threat to human life or public health; provided, however, that such deployment shall be strictly limited to the execution of core life-saving or environmental safety functions, shall never extend to administrative, logistical, or standard operational duties, and shall immediately terminate upon the cessation of the acute life threat — regardless of whether such substituting personnel belong to an agency that remains funded or possesses alternative federal, state, or statutory authority during a partial or total government shutdown.

Subsection 1–4(c): Absolute Ceilings on Automated Workflows and Digital Strikebreaking. The prohibitions established across the entirety of this Section shall further apply to the direct or indirect procurement or activation of automated workflows, third-party software-as-a-service, or algorithmically driven external platforms intended to offset or absorb the operational deficit caused by the labor action. Under no circumstances shall any pre-existing automated system, algorithmic process, artificial intelligence framework, software platform, or digital workflow be permitted to increase its operational output, workload capacity, task volume, autonomous execution, transaction throughput, decision-making authority, or functional utilization beyond the average daily parameters recorded during the ninety calendar days immediately preceding the commencement of the labor action, or during the corresponding seasonal calendar period in the preceding fiscal year, whichever baseline reflects a lower threshold of automated throughput. Any operational reliance on such systems that bypasses or substitutes for the historical human verification, modification, or supervision of the striking bargaining unit shall constitute a per se violation of this Section.

Section 2: Enforcement Clause

Section 2. Congress shall have the power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation, including the establishment of procedures, protections, and remedies necessary to implement the rights set forth herein. Notwithstanding this enforcement power, the provisions of Section 1 of this article shall be self-executing and shall take effect regardless of the enactment of implementing legislation.

Section 3: Essential Services Work Stoppage Restrictions

Section 3.

3–1: Categorization of Essential Services and Congressional Oversight. The rights guaranteed by Section 1 of this article shall not extend to labor actions within essential services where a temporary work stoppage would pose an immediate, direct, and severe threat to public safety, national defense, or national security. For purposes of this article, essential services shall be strictly limited to law enforcement, firefighting services, emergency medical personnel, air traffic controllers, aviation security personnel, members of the armed forces, and the direct operational, cybersecurity, and digital infrastructure personnel required to maintain the continuous functioning of nuclear, electrical, water treatment, and natural gas utility systems. Congress shall retain the authority to regulate labor actions by employees in these designated essential services and members of the armed forces to protect national defense, national security, and the public welfare.

3–2: Automatic Dissolution of Strike Restrictions Upon Compensation Default. Notwithstanding such classifications, any restriction on labor actions under this section shall immediately dissolve, and the full right to engage in strikes, work stoppages, or the withholding of labor protected under Section 1 shall be restored, if the employing public or private entity fails to provide timely, scheduled compensation in full on the established date of payroll. For the purposes of this article, a failure to deliver full compensation within forty-eight hours of the calendar day on which payroll is contractually or statutorily due shall constitute an absolute default; provided, however, that this window shall extend to seventy-two hours solely in verified events of systemic, third-party banking infrastructure failure or widespread digital network outages independent of the employer's control; provided further that the employer has otherwise initiated and fully funded the payroll obligation. Under no circumstances shall a lapse in legislative appropriations, a government shutdown, or an employer's internal administrative error qualify for said seventy-two-hour extension. For the purposes of this article, a lapse in federal, state, or municipal appropriations, resulting in a government shutdown, the temporary suspension of agency funding, or the imposition of mandatory unpaid furloughs, shall constitute a per se failure to provide timely, scheduled compensation, and no affected employee shall be compelled to perform labor without contemporaneous, full fiscal compensation.

3–3: Strict Construction of Essential Personnel Duties and Protection of Auxiliary Roles. For the purposes of this Section, the classification of 'essential services' shall be strictly construed based on the specific, real-time duties performed by the employee, rather than job titles, civil service rankings, or broad agency designations. Classification under this Section shall require a showing that the specific employee's immediate absence creates a direct, un-attenuated threat of physical destruction or loss of life, independent of general economic or operational inconvenience. The inclusion of digital infrastructure and cybersecurity personnel shall apply solely to those individuals whose immediate, un-substituted absence would cause an instantaneous and catastrophic failure of utility grids, water sanitation, or nuclear safety systems; wherein such failure would result in immediate bodily harm, loss of life, or widespread biological contamination. Under no circumstances shall this classification be expanded by the United States, any State, or political subdivision thereof to encompass general administrative, technical support, educational, or auxiliary public sector roles.

Section 4: Critical Infrastructure & Supply Chain Mandates

Section 4.

4–1: Minimum Operational Mandates for Supply Chain Preservation. Congress shall have the authority to require that employees in critical transport, logistics, maritime ports, freight rail, commercial aviation, and infrastructure sectors maintain minimum operations during a labor dispute solely to prevent an imminent threat to public safety or a catastrophic collapse of the national supply chain vital to human survival; provided, however, that during any active labor action affecting these sectors, all participating entities shall preserve the continuous, safety-compliant handling, temperature-monitoring, pressure-relief regulation, and atmospheric ventilation of cryogenic refrigerants, hazardous cooling agents, volatile chemical assets, Class 9 lithium-ion battery systems, and critical petroleum products — including but not limited to solid carbon dioxide (UN1845/dry ice), refrigerated liquid nitrogen (UN1977), Class 2.3 toxic inhalation gases, Class 5.2 thermally unstable organic peroxides, Class 9 lithium-ion cell configurations (UN3480/UN3481), Class 3 bulk refined petroleum or aviation fuels, high-amperage industrial electrical couplers, critical fleet transport or heavy manufacturing components, and any analogous hazardous materials, volatile chemical assets, or advanced energy storage technologies classified under current or subsequent federal or international transit safety standards — to prevent cargo degradation, explosive atmospheric decomposition, pressure-induced package rupture, regional energy grid starvation, thermal runaway propagation, widespread electrical infrastructure disconnection, systemic vehicle fleet depletion, or crew asphyxiation in confined transit compartments.

4–2: Funding Pre-Requisites for Minimum Mandates and Emergency Appropriations. However, if a labor action in these sectors is triggered by an employer’s default on timely, scheduled payroll, Congress may invoke a minimum operational mandate only if it simultaneously guarantees full, immediate payment of all affected personnel through emergency appropriations. Absent the enactment and fulfillment of such immediate funding, all operational mandates and restrictions on work stoppages under this Section shall dissolve, and the full protections and rights established in Section 1 shall apply without qualification.

Section 5: Immunity from Civil Liability and Injunctions

Section 5.

5–1: Complete Shield from Tort Liabilities and Restrictions on Judicial Injunctions. No labor organization, collective bargaining unit, or individual officer or member thereof shall be held civilly liable in any court of the United States or any State for economic damages, lost profits, or business disruption resulting from a protected labor action under this article. No court of the United States or any State shall have jurisdiction to issue temporary restraining orders, preliminary injunctions, or permanent injunctions to halt, delay, or restrict any labor action protected under Section 1, except upon a clear showing of imminent, physical violence directly perpetrated by striking personnel causing immediate bodily injury or active property destruction. The manifestation of widespread economic disruption, operational delays, financial losses, supply chain friction, or structural budgetary deficits shall never be construed by any court as constituting physical violence, public danger, or a constructive threat to physical safety under this Section.

5–2: Corporate and Successor Accountability, Anti-Retaliation Presumptions, and Mandatory Judicial Status Quo Orders. The prohibitions under this Section shall bind the employer without limitation, including any parent corporations, domestic or international subsidiaries, shell companies, contracted third-party entities, or automated technological frameworks and artificial intelligence systems operating to substitute for the duties of the affected workforce. Furthermore, any mass layoff, departmental elimination, discretionary elimination of program funding, targeted legislative defunding of specific bargaining units, or selective workforce reduction initiated by an employer or by a legislative or governing body during an active labor dispute or within ninety days of its resolution shall carry a rebuttable presumption of unlawful labor retaliation, regardless of whether such actions are attributed to a power grid failure, natural disaster, or other emergency pretext. Courts of the United States or any State shall have jurisdiction and a mandatory constitutional obligation to issue immediate interim injunctive relief to freeze such layoffs or funding cuts pending the final adjudication of a full administrative audit of the employer's financial necessity. The core fact-finding and administrative audit shall be executed by a designated federal or state labor regulatory agency, or an independent special master appointed by the court, the preliminary phase of which must be concluded within thirty calendar days of filing; provided that the court finds sufficient cause to continue the interim freeze; and provided further that the final audit must be fully adjudicated within ninety calendar days, during which time all affected employees shall remain fully employed with undisturbed compensation and benefits.

Section 6: Effect Delay Clause

Section 6. This article of amendment shall take effect six months after the date of ratification; providing states, employers, and employees adequate time to adjust to the rights and obligations established herein. Upon the date of ratification and during this interim period, no employer or State shall take any retaliatory or adverse employment action against employees, nor execute layoffs, nor alter pension, insurance, or re-employment rights, in anticipation of the protections established herein. This article shall be entirely self-executing, with its interim anti-retaliation protections becoming immediately operative upon ratification, and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation. This absolute constitutional firewall safeguards all accrued pensions, insurance plans, and benefits, and it shall remain non-waivable during any fiscal crisis or emergency pretext.

Legal & technical breakdown

Section 1: The Right to Work Stoppage

Constitutional Purpose: Codifies foundational labor strike rights and establishes an anti-scabbing framework.

Intended Outcome: Secures public and private sector strike rights (1-1); limits lockouts to 14 days to prevent companies from starving out unions (1-2); protects vested pensions, health benefits, and seniority from employer retaliation (1-3); and completely bans human personnel substitutions, out-of-jurisdiction police swaps, and the deployment of "algorithmic/AI scabs" beyond a 90-day pre-strike benchmark (1-4).

  • Punitive state laws like Texas Government Code § 617.003 and Florida Statute § 447.505 becomes overridden by this amendment.
  • Strike-breaking scabs, either physical (i.e. National Guard or military reserves) or digital (i.e. AI, automated workflows), becomes unconstitutional.
  • Executive and governmental overreach loophole — including the President deploying ICE agents to temporarily substitute unpaid TSA workers at major U.S. airports during the DHS shutdown despite they were untrained to handle airport security — becomes unconstitutional. This happened in early 2026, with passengers waiting at extremely long lines at major U.S. airports (including IAH and ATL airports) to reach their flights, causing significant delays.

Section 2: Enforcement Clause

Constitutional Purpose: Establishes federal labor implementation powers.

Intended Outcome: Authorizes Congress to build extensive worker protection frameworks while guaranteeing that Section 1 remains fully self-executing and legally binding even in the absence of federal legislation.

Section 3: Essential Services Carve-Out Clause

Constitutional Purpose: Minimizes catastrophic public safety failures while protecting worker compensation.

Intended Outcome: Restricts strikes only within a highly narrow list of life-safety fields (3-1); automatically dissolves all strike bans if an employer defaults on payroll for more than 48 hours during funding disputes or shutdowns (3-2); and strictly prevents agencies from expanding the "essential" tag to general administrative or auxiliary roles (3-3).

Section 4: Critical Infrastructure & Supply Chain Mandates

Constitutional Purpose: Protects the national supply chain, public safety corridors, and life-sustaining logistics networks during profound macroeconomic or geopolitical crises.

Intended Outcome: Permits Congress to require baseline minimum operational standards in vital transport, maritime ports, freight rail, and hazardous cargo nodes solely to prevent human survival catastrophes, regional energy grid starvation, electrochemical thermal runaway, and chemical, petroleum, or cryogenic transit accidents; provided, the federal government simultaneously funds full emergency appropriations under Section 4–2 to pay the affected workers.

Section 5: Immunity from Civil Liability and Injunctions

Constitutional Purpose: Shuts down the judicial weaponization of courts against labor unions.

Intended Outcome: Grants total immunity to unions from corporate tort damages or lost profits (5-1), strips courts of jurisdiction to issue anti-strike injunctions, and forces a mandatory judicial freeze on mass layoffs, program defunding, or corporate shell reorganizations during or within 90 days of a labor dispute (5-2).

Section 6: Effect Delay Clause

Constitutional Purpose: Sets a smooth administrative adjustment window.

Intended Outcome: Delays standard operational effects for six months to allow unions and management to rewrite bargaining contracts, while instantly enacting an ironclad, self-executing anti-retaliation firewall to protect pensions and benefits during the transition.

Overall Constitutional Philosophy (Economic Countervailing Power)

The LSA is built on the philosophy that political democracy is hollow without industrial democracy. It establishes the right to strike as an un-waivable constitutional power, recognizing that the ability to collectively withhold labor is the primary mechanism working-class citizens possess to check concentrated corporate and administrative capital.

Underlying Philosophy (Anti-Coercion & Algorithmic Protection)

The amendment anticipates 21st-century corporate and executive stratagems. It views the deployment of uncertified public personnel, state militias, or automated generative AI systems during a strike not as "neutral operations," but as highly coercive, dangerous acts of physical and digital strikebreaking that undermine human labor value.

Societal Goals

  • Eliminating Judicial Strike-Breaking: Stripping courts of the power to issue corporate-backed injunctions, asset freezes, or financial tort damages against labor unions.
  • Securing Shutdown Protections: Guaranteeing that public civil servants can never be forced into unpaid labor during legislative funding standoffs or government shutdowns.
  • Neutralizing Algorithmic Scabbing: Implementing rigid 90-day pre-strike operational caps on AI and automated systems to prevent tech monopolies from automating away striking workers.
  • Preventing Economic Retaliation: Enacting mandatory judicial freezes on mass layoffs or sudden departmental defunding carried out in the wake of union actions.

🛠️ LSA Evidence Matrix: Constitutional Defenses Against Modern Labor Suppression

🏛️ Design Principle: Structured Continuity

The Labor Stoppage Amendment is built on the principle of balanced governance. While it establishes unprecedented protections for worker sovereignty and outlaws digital and human strikebreaking, it explicitly rejects operational chaos. Through carefully calibrated intervention triggers in Sections 2, 3, and 4, the text empowers Congress — and Congress alone — to mandate binding arbitration, define narrow public safety exemptions, and enforce minimum supply-chain operational mandates. This ensures that the nation's critical infrastructure remains stable and resilient, even during the most intense labor disputes.

⚾ Note on Scope: Why Professional Sports are Excluded

While the expiration of the Major League Baseball (MLB) Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) on December 1, 2026, presents a clear threat of an offseason lockout, this amendment deliberately excludes professional sports leagues from its mandatory intervention triggers. The emergency mechanisms in Sections 2, 3, and 4 are strictly reserved for critical national infrastructure, public safety, and life-sustaining supply chains. Elevating commercial entertainment to the status of an essential service would dilute the amendment's legal gravity and risk corporate weaponization of legislative mandates against player unions.

Theoretical Framework in Crisis Management (Sections 3 & 4)

1. The Relationship: Brains vs. Hazards

  • Section 3 (The Human Variable): This section legally defines and regulates the personnel — the essential, emergency, and highly skilled frontline workers (like petroleum engineers, locomotive engineers, and automated dock technicians). It outlines their rights, classifications, and basic parameters during a crisis.
    —
  • Section 4 (The Physical Load): This section defines the assets and hazards — the high-amperage couplers, UN3480/UN3481 lithium systems, Class 3 refined fuels, and cryogenic agents.

How they relate: Section 4 provides the strict, science-based justification for activating Section 3. Under the LSA, the federal government cannot declare workers "essential" under Section 3 just to save a corporation's stock price. They can only invoke Section 3 if the specific physical, thermodynamic, or logistical threats listed in Section 4 are explicitly triggered.

2. The Link: The Skeleton Crew Matrix

Sections 3 and 4 link together through the mechanism of the Surgical Skeleton Crew.

When a massive industrial strike occurs under Section 1, standard commercial commerce stops. However, Section 4 acts as a sensor that detects high-stakes infrastructure bottlenecks. The moment it detects cargo that risks thermal runaway, package rupture, or grid starvation, it activates Section 3 to deploy a highly specialized, minimal workforce.

For example, in a heavy manufacturing strike (Exhibit J):

  • Section 4 outlines that a total freeze on transit components will cause systemic fleet depletion for emergency vehicles.
    —
  • Section 3 immediately translates this into action by isolating the specific, non-supervisory aerospace and transit engineers needed to process only those parts. The rest of the factory workers remain on the picket line, maintaining maximum financial leverage over the company.

3. The Translation: Turning "Forced Labor" into "Sovereign Duty"

Historically, when the U.S. government used emergency powers (like the Taft-Hartley Act) to force "essential workers" back to work, it translated to a loss of worker sovereignty — crushing the strike completely.

The LSA completely translates this dynamic through a beautiful constitutional compromise:

  • The Safety Mandate: Section 4 requires that the continuous, climate-controlled handling of volatile assets must occur. Section 3 translates this into a binding duty for the skeleton crew to maintain those specific operations.
    —
  • The Funding Firewall (Section 4–2 via Section 3): To ensure this duty is never exploited as forced corporate labor, Section 4's funding mechanism translates straight into the workers' pockets under Section 3. The federal government is constitutionally mandated to pay these essential emergency crews using immediate federal appropriations.

Instead of treating "essential operations" as a single vague concept, the amendment splits them into two specialized gears: Sovereign Enforcement vs. Industrial Physics.

👮 Section 3: Essential Services Work Stoppage Restrictions

  • The Focus: Human-to-Human Public Safety & Sovereign Order. * The Scope: This section governs public-facing emergency services whose physical absence would instantly trigger civic collapse or lawlessness—specifically law enforcement, structural firefighting, emergency medical technicians (EMTs), and active military defense.
    —
  • The Legal Mechanism: Under Section 3, these specific workers have tailored strike restrictions because their primary function is immediate, active crisis intervention. A city can survive a manufacturing halt, but it cannot survive 48 hours without a police force or fire department without descending into immediate civil chaos.

⚙️ Section 4: Critical Infrastructure and Supply Chain Mandates

  • The Focus: Thermodynamic Hazard Mitigation & Material Flow.
    —
  • The Scope: This section does not deal with active law enforcement or policing. Instead, it governs the microscopic and macroscopic bottlenecks of industrial physics—the Class 9 lithium batteries, Class 3 refined fuels, high-amperage industrial couplers, and heavy transit supply chains.
    —
  • The Legal Mechanism: This section does not ban strikes in these sectors. Instead, it allows workers to strike, but mandates that a surgical, minimal operational standard be maintained solely to prevent physical catastrophes (like a refinery explosion or systemic emergency fleet depletion).

🤝 How Sections 3 & 4 Interlock During a Dispute

When a major nationwide dispute or natural disaster strikes, Sections 3 and 4 handshake to keep society structurally stable:

  1. The Material Triggers the Labor: If a freight rail strike occurs, Section 4 flags that volatile assets (like Class 2.3 toxic inhalation gases or bulk aviation fuel) are sitting unmonitored in a yard.
    —
  2. The Personnel Translation: Because a Section 4 physical hazard perimeter is tripped, Section 3 provides the regulatory authority to mandate that a specialized skeleton crew of rail technicians stay on the job.
    —
  3. The Civil Protection Firewall: Simultaneously, standard Section 3 emergency personnel (like police and firefighters) remain fully active on the streets, ensuring that if a supply chain bottleneck does cause a localized utility failure, emergency services are structurally positioned to manage the public safety fallout.

📊 The Comprehensive LSA Functional Matrix

🛡️ Importance of the Effect Delay Clause (Section 6)

Historically, when monumental structural shifts are ratified (like the Twentieth Amendment or major labor updates), a legal vacuum opens up between the moment the vote is certified and the moment the law officially becomes active. During that exact "interim window," bad-actor corporations and hostile state regulators naturally rush to execute preemptive strikes — firing union organizers, stripping pensions, altering healthcare benefits, or executing mass preventative layoffs to gut the union's power before the new law protects them. By splitting Section 6 into a Delayed Operational Phase (6 months) and an Immediate Self-Executing Firewall, the constitutional text perfectly solves this transition hazard.

🛡️ Section 6 Architectural Breakdown

  • "This article of amendment shall take effect six months after the date of ratification..."
    —
    • The Strategy: This acts as a stabilization buffer. It prevents immediate structural shock to the national supply chain. It gives employers, states, and unions an exact 6-month window to rewrite collective bargaining agreements, align payrolls, and establish the specialized Section 3 and Section 4 skeleton crew matrices without interrupting active infrastructure.
      —
  • "...no employer or State shall take any retaliatory or adverse employment action... nor execute layoffs, nor alter pension, insurance, or re-employment rights, in anticipation of the protections established herein."
    —
    • The Strategy: This completely freezes the status quo. It neutralizes the exact corporate playbooks used during major historic shifts (like the 1930s New Deal rollouts) where companies scrambled to rewrite contracts before the federal government could stop them.
      —
  • "This article shall be entirely self-executing, with its interim anti-retaliation protections becoming immediately operative upon ratification, and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation."
    —
    • The Strategy: This is the legal hammer. Under U.S. constitutional law, if an amendment is not labeled "self-executing," it remains completely toothless until Congress passes a separate statute to enforce it. By explicitly declaring it self-executing, a worker at an Alief ISD school or an engineer at a Texas refinery who faces an adverse contract change can bypass a stalled Congress entirely. They can walk straight into a federal court on Day 1 after ratification and get an immediate judicial injunction to freeze the employer's retaliation.

📊 Matrix Integration — Section 6 Entry

The reason why I introduce this constitutional amendment

I believe public and private sector employees should be allowed to go on strike for reasons of labor disputes without facing state severe state-level sanctions, such as the forfeiture of earned pensions, healthcare access, and future re-employment rights. Simultaneously, owners should also be allowed to impose lockouts, also for labor disputes.

The Texas Government Code § 617, specifically 617.003, prohibits public sector employees (including staff and faculty members that work in schools or public colleges [i.e. University of Houston, Houston City College]) in the state of Texas from going on strike or face severe penalties of forfeiture by state governments. Not just Texas, but also Florida (Florida Statutes § 447.505). So, I want to override these state statutes with the Labor Stoppage Amendment (LSA) I've been thinking about to to shield labor unions and empower them to exercise their collective leverage whenever there are labor disputes.

I oppose and criticize the illegality of workers' (either public or private sector) from striking without facing state government penalties in some states. The fear of going on strike for public sector employees would be a severe penalty of forfeiture of pension, benefits, and re-employment rights.

The purpose of the Labor Stoppage Amendment (LSA) is to allow workers, either public or private sector, at any state to go on strike without facing severe state penalties. In fact, this will allow the leverage of collective bargaining power of a union of employees and employers. Also, I allow employers to retain the right to impose lockouts for labor dispute reasons under the circumstances of this amendment.

In addition to public and private workers having the right to go on strike whenever there is a labor dispute, I explicitly target and close dangerous administrative loopholes. This includes preventing raw executive overreach during government shutdowns — such as the recent DHS impasse where untrained personnel were deployed to replace unpaid aviation security workers — as well as the predatory deployment of automated systems and AI as digital scabs to undermine striking personnel.

In this constitutional amendment, I choose not to include the sunset clause, which would give states in the nation a limited amount of time to ratify passed amendments. So, by excluding the sunset clause, I choose to give states flexibility upon passage by Congress on legislative discussions to ratify this constitutional amendment on granting workers in a public or private sector setting the right to strike.

Also, in this constitutional amendment, I choose to include the Effect Delay Clause, which is defined in Section 6. I want this amendment to take effect in 6 months after a required number of states ratified the amendment, and give them adequate time and flexibility to adjust on new labor settings. I will also not allow employers, especially whenever they are hostile, to executively impose mass layoffs nor alter pension, insurance, and re-employment rights during this 6-month period.

Constitutional amendments require broad public support and careful national debate. While the Labor Stoppage Amendment (LSA) may be controversial, I welcome constructive comments, criticism, and proposed changes from the public as part of the constitutional process. This is one of the hardest and most comprehensive constitutional amendments to produce.

Steps to take this amendment into law

Once I finalize the draft of this constitutional amendment with some help from other people, legal scholars, or lawmakers by means of review and evaluation, then I would send this amendment article to Washington, D.C., at the U.S. Capitol Hill for Congress to attempt to pass this amendment.

First, under Article V of the United States Constitution in terms of getting the amendment into law, Congress must vote 2/3 in both the House of Representatives and the Senate to pass this constitutional amendment.

  • 290 out of 435 House of Representatives are required to pass
  • 67 out of 100 Senators are required to pass

Alternatively, under Article V of the United States Constitution, a national convention can be called on proposing this constitutional amendment if 2/3 (34 out of 50 states) of state legislatures apply to Congress to do so. This method was never utilized in U.S. history.

Once this constitutional amendment is passed by Congress, then the next step is ratification, which requires at least 3/4 of the states to ratify this constitutional amendment.

  • 38 out of 50 States are required to ratify

If this Labor Stoppage Amendment (LSA) is ratified into the United States Constitution, then it would become the 28th Amendment to the United States Constitution (or 29th Amendment if the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) is officially ratified and certified first that it was in legal limbo for decades since expiration). This constitutional amendment would override state government codes, which prohibits public sector workers (all employees and employers) from striking or organizing work stoppages without facing state penalties like forfeiture, including as outlined in Texas Government Code § 617. This amendment would override Texas Government Code § 617, allowing public sector workers to strike, especially whenever there are labor disputes.

Sponsorship List

I will add a bullet list to credit people here who sponsor or co-sponsor this constitutional amendment. People on this list would mostly be politicians; they could be legislators serving in Congress.

???

NOTE: If you want me to credit you on this list on this constitutional amendment article, then leave a comment on this article that you are sponsoring or co-sponsoring this amendment on workers' right to labor work stoppage without facing state penalties.

  • To be added upon user comments.

Supporters

I will add a bullet list to credit people here who support this constitutional amendment, instead of sponsorship which only applies to politicians. People on this list would mostly be citizens who are not politicians or serving in political office.

NOTE: If you want me to credit you on this list on this constitutional amendment article, then leave a comment on this article that you are supporting this amendment on workers' right to labor work stoppage without facing state penalties.

item.title: Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment (PGPA)
item.dc:creator: allenacnguyen
item.content:encoded:
I, Allen Nguyen — an independent citizen from Houston, TX, and a Summa Cum Laude graduate from the University of Houston with a Bachelor of Science in Digital Media degree — introduce a constitutional amendment that would stop extreme state partisan gerrymandering over rigging congressional and legislative districts in states to solve democratic and electoral fairness.

Amendment Slogan

"Voters Choose Politicians. Not the Other Way Around."

Update 7/6/2026: Added "Definitions" section; reworked constitutional language.

Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment

Section 1: Prohibition of the Intent of Partisan Gerrymandering

Section 1. All legislative bodies covered under this article shall be elected exclusively from single-member geographic districts, unless an alternative proportional representation framework is explicitly authorized by Congress. Districts established for the election of Members of the United States House of Representatives, members of the lower chamber of any State legislature, and members of the upper chamber of any State legislature, shall not be drawn, altered, or maintained for the purpose of favoring or disadvantaging a political party, its candidates, or any coalition of voters or supporters based on shared political alignment.

Section 2: Prohibition of the Outcome of Undue Partisan Advantage

Section 2. No State, political subdivision, officer, commission, legislature, or other governmental authority shall enact, approve, or implement any congressional, State House, or State Senate redistricting plan that has the purpose or effect of granting an undue partisan advantage, as defined in Section 5 of this article, or disadvantage to any political party or to any group of citizens based on their voting history or political alignment.

Section 3: Judicial Review, Remedies, and Evidence Clause

Section 3. Any redistricting plan for the United States House of Representatives, a State House of Representatives or equivalent lower legislative chamber, or a State Senate or equivalent upper legislative chamber shall be subject to judicial review. Federal and State courts shall have authority to determine whether a plan complies with this article and to provide appropriate remedies, including the invalidation of unlawful districts and the adoption or supervision of lawful replacement plans; provided that any judicially adopted map must maximize mathematical neutrality, minimize measurable partisan asymmetry, satisfy all applicable constitutional requirements, and perform no worse than the median of independently generated neutral ensemble maps according to the standards established by this article over all rejected alternatives. In determining compliance, courts may consider statistical evidence, mathematical modeling, algorithmic simulations, artificial intelligence modeling, machine learning analysis, ensemble map analyses, historical patterns, expert analysis, computational modeling, transparent and independently reproducible algorithmic methods, peer-reviewed methodologies where reasonably practicable, and any other relevant indicators of partisan bias or mathematical neutrality.

Section 4: Neutral Standards and Counting Clause

Section 4. In reviewing redistricting plans, courts shall apply neutral and objective standards consistent with constitutional fairness. The primary criteria for compliance shall be electoral fairness, the minimization of partisan bias, and the proportionality of seats to votes as measured across a range of reasonable electoral outcomes, with mathematical neutrality as defined in Section 5 of this article. The criteria of electoral fairness and mathematical proportionality of seats to votes shall constitute the highest constitutional standards governing the review of districting plans. Where geographic compactness, contiguity, or respect for political subdivisions conflict with or produce a statistically significant deviation from mathematical proportionality, such traditional criteria must yield to ensure proportional fairness. Consistent with these primary criteria, courts may consider geographic compactness, contiguity, respect for political subdivisions, and respect for communities of interest. Any map layout resulting in a deviation from mathematical proportionality or partisan symmetry that exceeds two standard deviations from the mean of the distribution of constitutionally compliant electoral outcomes generated through independently verified, transparent, and non-partisan neutral ensemble modeling, as defined in Section 5 of this article, shall be unconstitutional, thereby leaving courts with no discretionary authority to validate maps displaying artificial partisan asymmetry measured across a historically grounded range of statewide electoral outcomes. Any artificial intelligence system, machine learning model, computational algorithm, or statistical methodology relied upon under this article shall be publicly disclosed, independently reproducible, auditable, and subject to adversarial examination by all parties before judicial consideration.

For the purposes of establishing population equality under this article, incarcerated individuals shall be counted at their last known legal residence prior to incarceration. Where a prior legal residence cannot be verified after an exhaustive, judicially verifiable audit, the individual shall be apportioned uniformly across all state districts entirely, rather than counted at the facility of incarceration; ensuring that under no circumstances or administrative default shall any such individual be counted or assigned to the population base of the political subdivision containing the facility of incarceration.

Section 5: Definitions

Section 5. For the purposes of this article:

'Mathematical neutrality' means the absence of statistically significant partisan asymmetry relative to the distribution of outcomes produced through independently verified neutral ensemble modeling.

'Neutral ensemble modeling' means the generation of a sufficiently large collection of constitutionally compliant districting plans through transparent, reproducible, non-partisan computational methods without regard to the expected electoral performance of any political party.

'Undue partisan advantage' means a statistically significant deviation from mathematical neutrality that cannot reasonably be explained by geography, constitutional requirements, or random variation.

Section 6: Enforcement Clause

Section 6. Congress shall have power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation. Such legislation may establish minimum national standards for congressional and State legislative redistricting, may regulate or prohibit the use of proprietary artificial intelligence technologies, machine learning systems, computational optimization algorithms, and substantially equivalent future technologies designed to optimize partisan advantage, and may authorize, require, or regulate independent redistricting commissions for the establishment of districts for the United States House of Representatives, State Houses of Representatives or equivalent lower legislative chambers, and State Senates or equivalent upper legislative chambers. Any independent redistricting commission authorized or required under this article shall be guaranteed non-discretionary public funding sufficient to fulfill its duties, and the selection process for its members shall be fully transparent, verifiable, and subject to expedited judicial review to prevent partisan capture.

Congress may require that all computational models, artificial intelligence systems, statistical software, source code where practicable, datasets, assumptions, and ensemble generation methodologies used in official redistricting be publicly documented and independently verifiable. All datasets, software, computational methods, assumptions, statistical analyses, and ensemble generation methodologies relied upon pursuant to this article shall be subject to public disclosure and independent inspection, except where nondisclosure is required by this Constitution or by other provisions of law enacted pursuant thereto.

Section 7: Effective Date and Frequency Clause

Section 7. This article shall take effect immediately upon ratification and shall immediately invalidate any non-compliant maps then in effect, regardless of when they were enacted, and shall apply to all districts for the United States House of Representatives, State Houses of Representatives or equivalent lower legislative chambers, and State Senates or equivalent upper legislative chambers thereafter. Districts covered under this article shall be established no more than once per decennial census cycle, except when strictly required by a court of competent jurisdiction to remedy a violation of law. This article shall be entirely self-executing and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation.

Legal & technical breakdown

Section 1: Prohibition of the Intent of Partisan Gerrymandering

Constitutional Purpose: Eliminates bad-faith political district intent and bans structural voting dilutes.

Intended Outcome: Mandates that all federal and state legislative elections occur exclusively via single-member geographic lines, completely banning state legislatures from drawing maps for the purpose of favoring or disadvantaging any political coalition or party alignment.

Section 2: Prohibition of the Outcome of Undue Partisan Advantage

Constitutional Purpose: Establishes a strict "effects-based" test that punishes the mathematical outcome of a rigged map, regardless of the mapmakers' stated intentions.

Intended Outcome: Banishes the implementation of any redistricting layout that grants an unfair partisan edge or disadvantage to any group based on voter history, closing the loophole where mapmakers claim a biased map was just an "accidental byproduct" of geography.

Section 3: Judicial Review, Remedies, and Evidence Clause

Constitutional Purpose: Completely overrules the Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) "political question" defense by creating a mandatory constitutional directive for judicial intervention.

Intended Outcome: Empowers federal and state courts to strike down illegal maps and implement neutral replacements, forces judicially adopted maps to meet or exceed the absolute median of fairness, and explicitly legitimizes modern data science, ensemble simulations, and machine learning models as valid legal evidence.

Section 4: Neutral Standards and Counting Clause

Constitutional Purpose: Establishes data science and the statistical Empirical Rule (±2σ) as the absolute supreme boundary governing American elections, while structurally outlawing prison gerrymandering.

Intended Outcome: Forces traditional map rules (like compactness) to yield to mathematical proportionality. Any map that deviates from neutrality by more than two standard deviations from the distribution mean is instantly unconstitutional, stripping judges of any bias-driven discretion. It additionally requires total transparency for all AI/algorithms used, and reassigns or uniformly distributes incarcerated individuals to protect urban population bases.

Section 5: Definitions

Constitutional Purpose: Anchors the key operational definitions of the amendment directly into the constitutional bedrock, completely preventing bad-faith legal actors from twisting the meaning of fairness.

Intended Outcome: Explicitly defines "mathematical neutrality," "neutral ensemble modeling," and "undue partisan advantage" as science-based concepts measured against thousands of computer-simulated neutral maps, creating an unbribable, legally binding dictionary for the courts.

Section 6: Enforcement Clause

Constitutional Purpose: Arms Congress with broad, uniform regulatory authority to enforce redistricting fairness across all fifty states and explicitly allows the mandate of independent commissions.

Intended Outcome: Gives Congress the power to outlaw proprietary "black box" optimization AI used by political operatives, guarantees non-discretionary public funding to independent commissions to protect them from partisan budget cuts, and mandates an open-source framework where all redistricting code, datasets, and assumptions are fully accessible to the public.

Section 7: Effective Date and Frequency Clause

Constitutional Purpose: Eliminates the transitional "grace period" that partisan actors historically exploit to lock in power before a major reform takes effect.

Intended Outcome: Automatically dissolves every non-compliant, gerrymandered map in the nation the exact moment the 38th state ratifies the amendment, limits map changes to exactly once per decade following the U.S. Census, and declares the article entirely self-executing so it cannot be stalled by an uncooperative Congress.

Overall Constitutional Purpose (Empirical & Mathematical Proportionality)

The PGPA approaches democratic legitimacy through the lens of objective structural mathematics. It explicitly rejects the notion that maps are a "political question" beyond judicial reach, establishing that a truly representative democracy must maintain a direct, measurable mathematical ratio between total popular votes cast and seats awarded.

Underlying Philosophy (Anti-Cartelization & Carceral Justice)

It targets the entrenchment of self-perpetuating political duopolies. It recognizes that political cartels use traditional geographic criteria as a smokescreen to rig maps, and weaponize incarcerated populations to inflate rural power, systematically stealing representation from diverse, urban centers.

Intended Societal Outcomes

  • Eradication of Rigged Maps: Overruling Rucho v. Common Cause to permanently authorize federal and state courts to strike down asymmetrical legislative districts using ensemble modeling.
  • Ending Prison Gerrymandering: Requiring incarcerated individuals to be counted at their last known legal residence, restoring millions of dollars in funding and true voting weight to their home communities.
  • Securing Independent Commissions: Establishing fully transparent independent redistricting bodies backed by non-discretionary public funding to eliminate insider map-drawing.
  • Enforcing Legislative Alignment: Ensuring that the composition of federal and state legislatures accurately mirrors the political will of the collective electorate, eliminating minority-party rule.

Exhibits leading to this amendment proposal

🏛️ Part I: Systemic & Structural Exploitation (7 Exhibits)

  • 📊 Exhibit A: Micro-Targeted Distortions and the Structural Disadvantage in Texas
  • ✂️ Exhibit B: The Dismantling of Competitive Urban Hubs in Tennessee
  • 🗺️ Exhibit C: The Executive-Driven Map Overhaul in Florida
  • ⛓️ Exhibit D: Prison Gerrymandering and Democratic Distortions
  • 🧑🏾 Exhibit E: Racial Vote Dilution and Partisan Cloaking
  • ⏱️ Exhibit F: Temporal Lock-Ins and Frequency Abuse
  • 📊 Exhibit G: Public Consensus vs. Structural Manipulation

🏛️ Part II: Localized Community-Level Disruption (2 Exhibits)

  • 🗺️ Exhibit H: Arbitrary Fragmenting and the Shuffling of Houston Communities
  • 🥊 Exhibit I: The Manufactured Inter-Party Clash in Texas’ 18th Congressional District

🏛️ Part I: Systemic & Structural Exploitation (7 Exhibits)

📊 Exhibit A: Micro-Targeted Distortions and the Structural Disadvantage in Texas

  • Context: In highly polarized, Republican-dominant states like Texas, mapmakers utilize sophisticated GIS software and historical voting data to engineer safe majorities. Despite major metropolitan areas shifting dynamically, map boundaries are explicitly drawn to isolate growing urban and suburban populations into hyper-packed minority-party districts while sprawling rural lines dilute the remainder, leaving opposition voters structurally locked out of competitive representation.
    —
  • PGPA Section: Section 1 (Prohibition of the Intent of Partisan Gerrymandering) & Section 2 (Prohibition of the Outcome of Undue Partisan Advantage).

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit A

The PGPA establishes a strict constitutional baseline to neutralize intentional systemic bias. Section 1 outlaws the deliberate, behind-closed-doors intent to map districts for political entrenchment, while Section 2 looks directly at empirical results. Together, they strip line-drawers of the ability to insulate their majorities from shifting demographics, ensuring that a political party’s legislative power directly mirrors its statewide popular support.

✂️ Exhibit B: The Dismantling of Competitive Urban Hubs in Tennessee

  • Context: Following the 2020 redistricting cycle, the state of Tennessee served as a textbook example of "cracking" an urban core. The historic, reliably Democratic 5th Congressional District in Nashville was sliced into three separate, sprawling rural districts. This structural manipulation erased a competitive urban seat overnight, absorbing city voters into deep rural blocks and rendering it statistically impossible for their preferred candidates to win.
    —
  • PGPA Section: Section 2 (Prohibition of the Outcome of Undue Partisan Advantage) & Section 4 (Neutral Standards and Counting Clause).

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit B

The overriding purpose here is to protect organic geographic communities from surgical, partisan bisection. Section 4 mandates strict, neutral mapping criteria that prioritize municipal boundaries and community cohesion over party advantage. When combined with the outcome metrics of Section 2, the amendment effectively bans the 'cracking' of metro areas to manufacture synthetic legislative supermajorities.

🗺️ Exhibit C: The Executive-Driven Map Overhaul in Florida

  • Context: During the 2022 redistricting cycle, Florida showcased the vulnerability of the mapmaking process to unilateral executive pressure. The executive branch bypassed traditional legislative compromises to push a highly aggressive map that dismantled historically protected minority-performing districts. This resulted in an unrepresentative statewide seat allocation that fundamentally distorted the balance of power relative to actual statewide voting behavior.
    —
  • PGPA Section: Section 3 (Judicial Review, Remedies, and Evidence Clause) & Section 5 (Enforcement Clause).

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit C

To counter hyper-partisan executive overreach, Section 3 creates an expedited, rigorous path for judicial review, dictating that courts may utilize modern statistical metrics as direct evidence of partisan bias. Section 6 (Enforcement Clause) provides federal courts and individual citizens with the self-executing legal teeth to instantly freeze and discard unconstitutional, skewed maps before they can be weaponized in upcoming elections.

⛓️ Exhibit D: Prison Gerrymandering and Democratic Distortions

  • Context: Prison gerrymandering represents a severe distortion of population metrics. Under traditional state rules, incarcerated individuals — who are disproportionately from urban areas and stripped of their voting rights — are counted as residents of the rural, white-dominant districts where they are confined. This artificially inflates the population totals of rural districts, granting outsized legislative power to those regions at the direct expense of the urban communities where the prisoners actually reside.
    —
  • PGPA Section: Section 4 (Neutral Standards and Counting Clause).

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit D

The PGPA permanently corrects this population padding through Section 4, which introduces strict, uniform counting standards. It constitutionally mandates that for the purposes of legislative line-drawing, incarcerated individuals must be counted at their last known permanent residential address prior to incarceration, rather than their place of confinement. This ensures legislative power is distributed based on actual voting constituencies, not carceral geography.

🧑🏾 Exhibit E: Racial Vote Dilution and Partisan Cloaking

  • Context: Mapmakers frequently weaponize partisan data to dilute minority voting strength, hiding behind the legal defense that they are targeting "Democrats" rather than racial minorities. By packing Black and Hispanic voters into a handful of overwhelming districts or cracking them across multiple white-dominated districts, states effectively suppress minority electoral leverage under the guise of ordinary partisan politics.
    —
  • PGPA Section: Section 1 (Prohibition of the Intent) & Section 2 (Prohibition of the Outcome).

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit E

The PGPA treats racial vote dilution and partisan gerrymandering as deeply intertwined constitutional evils. By establishing that any undue partisan outcome is a per se violation under Section 2, the amendment eliminates the loophole where mapmakers hide behind partisan labels to justify the systemic erasure of minority voting power. If a map dilutes a community's political voice, it is constitutionally invalid — full stop.

⏱️ Exhibit F: Temporal Lock-Ins and Frequency Abuse

  • Context: To maintain power indefinitely, entrenched majorities frequently abuse redistricting timelines. When a court strikes down a map, or when a mid-decade power shift occurs, parties attempt to redraw maps repeatedly outside of the standard decennial census cycle to continuously optimize their partisan advantage and exhaust civil rights litigators.
    —
  • PGPA Section: Section 7 (Effective Date and Frequency Clause).

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit F

Section 7 acts as a strict temporal regulator. It dictates that district boundaries may only be drawn once per decennial census cycle, unless expressly ordered by a federal court as a remedy for a constitutional violation. This stops defensive, mid-decade map-churning and gives voters structural stability, ensuring that politicians cannot continuously alter the rules of engagement.

📊 Exhibit G: Public Consensus vs. Structural Manipulation

Context: The Deepening Democratic Deficit

This exhibit contrasts a rare, overwhelming national consensus with the aggressive escalation of mid-decade partisan redistricting. While the American electorate is structurally polarized on many cultural issues, opposition to partisan gerrymandering is almost entirely unified. According to national data, 71% of all Americans support a total ban on line-drawing that favors a specific political party. This opposition bridges the partisan divide with remarkable consistency:

  • Democrats: 74% opposition
  • Independents: 70% opposition
  • Republicans: 69% opposition

Despite this clear mandate from the populace, self-perpetuating legislative majorities in states like Texas, North Carolina, Florida, and Ohio have actively ignored public protests. By executing voluntary, mid-decade map redraws leading into the 2026 midterm cycles, these political cartels have entrenched minority-party rule and forced high-profile incumbent-pairing clashes—such as the artificial pairing of senior Representative Al Green and Christian Menefee in Houston's redrawn 18th congressional district.

Relevant PGPA Sections

  • Section 1 (Prohibition of Intent): Outlaws the drawing or maintaining of districts designed to favor or disadvantage a political coalition, aligning the supreme law of the land with the 71% national consensus.
    —
  • Section 3 (Judicial Review & Evidence Clause): Provides the legal mechanism for citizens to use statistical modeling to prove when public will is being subverted by gerrymandered lines.
    —
  • Section 7 (Frequency Clause): Directly addresses the mid-decade redistricting weapon by restricting map adjustments strictly to once per decennial census cycle, neutralizing the exact tactics that sparked the modern nationwide protests.

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit G

The Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment (PGPA) is the direct constitutional answer to a nation in protest. When over seventy percent of Americans — regardless of party alignment — declare that rigged maps are an explicit threat to democratic legitimacy, the Constitution can no longer remain silent. By anchoring district design in empirical, mathematical proportionality and banning the chaotic disruption of mid-decade redraws, the PGPA strips political cartels of the pen and restores supreme sovereignty back to the voters. It transforms an overwhelming national consensus into an ironclad, un-waivable civil right.

🏛️ Part II: Localized & Community-Level Disruption (2 Exhibits)

🗺️ Exhibit H: Arbitrary Fragmenting and the Shuffling of Houston Communities

  • Context: Ahead of the 2026 election cycle, partisan mapmakers in Texas instituted voluntary mid-decade lines that radically reshuffled reliable voting bases in the Houston metroplex. Neighborhoods historically situated in the deeply competitive or left-leaning 9th Congressional District (represented by Rep. Al Green [D-TX]) were arbitrarily split and pushed into the adjacent 7th Congressional District (represented by Rep. Lizzie Fletcher [D-TX]). This structural displacement disrupts local organizing hubs, severs established constituent-representative relationships, and treats local communities like geographical chess pieces to manipulate surrounding suburban voting margins.
    —
  • PGPA Section: Section 1 (Prohibition of the Intent of Partisan Gerrymandering) & Section 2 (Prohibition of the Outcome of Undue Partisan Advantage).

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit H

The PGPA ensures structural stability for localized voting communities. Section 1 outlaws the deliberate alterations of district borders intended to dilute or shuffle voter groups based on political alignment. By removing the legislative power to carve up neighborhoods to protect safe suburban margins, the amendment protects local constituent continuity.

🥊 Exhibit I: The Manufactured Inter-Party Clash in Texas’ 18th Congressional District

  • Context: The weaponization of mid-decade redistricting in Texas culminated in a rare, high-stakes incumbent-versus-incumbent battle during the May 2026 primary runoffs. Mapmakers engineered a significant structural shift by drawing a major portion of the old 9th District into the deep-blue 18th Congressional District. This double-bunking forced 10-term veteran Rep. Al Green (D-TX) into a direct, zero-sum primary clash against newly elected freshman Rep. Christian Menefee (D-TX). By forcing two sitting Democrats into a single geographic boundary, the gerrymander successfully eliminated one of the state's most senior federal representatives, using internal party friction to dilute a metro hub's overall institutional leverage in Congress.
    —
  • PGPA Section: Section 1 (Prohibition of the Intent of Partisan Gerrymandering) & Section 4 (Neutral Standards and Counting Clause).

Intent of the Amendment: Exhibit I

The PGPA neutralizes the tactical use of 'incumbent pairing' to eliminate political opposition. Under the data standards of Section 4, a map that shifts veteran representatives into identical boundaries to manufacture a primary conflict would trigger a massive deviation from an independently generated neutral ensemble. Because the resulting layout falls outside two standard deviations from the distribution mean, the map would be ruled unconstitutional, protecting veteran and emerging representatives alike from synthetic erasure.

📊🏛️ The PGPA Portfolio Evaluation Matrix: Part I

📊🏛️ The PGPA Portfolio Evaluation Matrix: Part II

🏛️ The Rucho Roadblock: What the Supreme Court Did

In Rucho v. Common Cause, the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that partisan gerrymandering is a "political question" beyond the reach of the federal courts.

Writing for the conservative majority, Chief Justice John Roberts admitted that gerrymandering was unjust and incompatible with democratic principles, but argued that:

  1. There was no clear, manageable constitutional standard to determine when ordinary political mapmaking crosses the line into "undue" or unconstitutional partisan manipulation.
    —
  2. The federal judiciary has no business acting as political managers or choosing between different theories of electoral fairness.

The Rucho Effect

The Supreme Court slammed the federal courthouse door shut on voters. It told citizens that if a map was rigged purely for partisan advantage (even if it was done with surgical, mathematical precision to lock one party out of power permanently), federal judges could not intervene.

🔨 How the PGPA Systematically Shatters Rucho

The text of this amendment is a direct, point-by-point refutation of Chief Justice Roberts’ majority opinion. It resolves every single legal anxiety the Court manufactured in 2019.

1. It Supplies the "Missing" Constitutional Baseline

  • The Rucho Argument: The Court claimed the Constitution doesn't provide a clear standard for "fairness."
    —
  • The PGPA Remedy: Section 1 (Prohibition of the Intent) and Section 2 (Prohibition of the Outcome) explicitly write that standard into the supreme law of the land. By constitutionally declaring that creating an asymmetrical partisan advantage is illegal, this eliminates the court’s excuse that they don't have a mandate to act.

2. It Legalizes and Mandates Mathematical Standards

  • The Rucho Argument: Roberts complained that political scientists' metrics (like the efficiency gap, partisan asymmetry, and declination curves) were too complex and fluid for judges to use as constitutional tests.
    —
  • The PGPA Remedy: Section 3 (Judicial Review, Remedies, and Evidence Clause) and Section 4 (Neutral Standards and Counting Clause) explicitly codify these statistical baselines. This amendment tells federal judges: "You do not have to guess. You are constitutionally authorized and required to accept peer-reviewed mathematical data as direct evidence of an illegal map."

3. It Overrides the "Political Question" Doctrine

  • The Rucho Argument: The Court ruled that because the Constitution gives state legislatures the primary power to draw lines, federal courts shouldn't meddle in political calculations.
    —
  • The PGPA Remedy: A constitutional amendment alters the ground rules. By establishing a federal prohibition, you strip state legislatures of their "sovereign right" to rig maps. Under Section 5 (Enforcement Clause), federal courts are granted the explicit "teeth" to issue instant injunctions, strike down state maps, and appoint neutral masters to redraw them.

🏛️ Jurisprudential Impact: Overruling Rucho v. Common Cause (2019)

In 2019, the Supreme Court abdicated its role as a constitutional guardian in Rucho v. Common Cause, holding that federal courts lack the authority to police partisan gerrymandering due to a lack of 'judicially manageable standards.'

Constitutional Counterweight: The PGPA directly overrules this precedent. By codifying strict empirical boundaries in Section 2 and explicitly legalizing advanced statistical modeling as admissible evidence under Section 3, the amendment forces the federal judiciary to reopen its doors to voters, converting a 'political question' into an ironclad, enforceable constitutional mandate.

How the PGPA Handles Seat Gains and Losses (The 1929 Act)

Whenever a state gains or loses congressional seats due to national population shifts under the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929, they are legally required to redraw their maps. Section 7 of the PGPA explicitly accounts for this by permitting map adjustments "once per decennial census cycle."

The PGPA does not interfere with how many seats a state receives; rather, it acts as a permanent, mathematical guardrail. Whether a state is drawing 5 districts or 40 districts, those boundaries must fall within the neutral 2σ ensemble distribution mean. The data science standards in the PGPA are fully elastic — they scale perfectly regardless of a state's seat count changing.

The Legal Transformation

The reason why I introduce this constitutional amendment

I believe partisan gerrymandering, which involves rigging congressional and legislative maps in several states for the purpose of extreme partisan advantage over the other, should be unconstitutional among thousands or millions of voters in the nation. We want to put an end to this gerrymandering scheme in several states across the nation.

The rigging of congressional and legislative maps in some Republican-dominant states like Texas, Tennessee, and Florida puts Democratic Party representation at a disadvantage ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

The purpose of the Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment (PGPA) is to prevent redistricting maps in favor of one dominant political party over the other for the purpose of democratic and electoral fairness among voters in several states. Any redrawn congressional or legislative maps in several states would be subject to judicial neutrality and review under Section 3, and redrawn congressional or legislative state maps would be approved or disapproved at the discretion of the federal and/or state-level judges based on evidence. Section 4 covers electoral fairness and proportionality when courts review redistricting plans. Section 5 covers the definitions for clarity purposes of this amendment article. Congress, under Section 6, will also have power to enforce and implement the provisions of this article by appropriate legislation that may include the establishment of independent redistricting commissions.

In this constitutional amendment, I choose not to include the sunset clause, which would give states in the nation a limited amount of time to ratify passed amendments. So, by excluding the sunset clause, I choose to give states flexibility upon passage by Congress on legislative discussions to ratify this constitutional amendment on preventing any gerrymandered maps in the future.

Also, in this constitutional amendment, I included the Effective Date and Frequency Clause, as covered in Section 7, to ensure that the amendment will take effect for the first redistricting cycle upon ratification; it could be the next decade or election or so. As for the frequency of redistricting, the purpose of congressional and state legislative redistricting should only occur once in a decade, unless when strictly required by a court of competent jurisdiction to remedy a violation of the law, in which case the redistricted maps could be used twice in a decade.

Constitutional amendments require broad public support and careful national debate. While the Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment (PGPA) may be controversial, I welcome constructive comments, criticism, and proposed changes from the public as part of the constitutional process. This is the hardest constitutional amendment to make to solve gerrymandering issues across several states for democratic and electoral fairness.

Steps to take this amendment into law

Once I finalize the draft of this constitutional amendment with some help from other people, legal scholars, or lawmakers by means of review and evaluation, then I would send this amendment article to Washington, D.C., at the U.S. Capitol Hill for Congress to attempt to pass this amendment.

First, under Article V of the United States Constitution in terms of getting the amendment into law, Congress must vote 2/3 in both the House of Representatives and the Senate to pass this constitutional amendment.

  • 290 out of 435 House of Representatives are required to pass
  • 67 out of 100 Senators are required to pass

Alternatively, under Article V of the United States Constitution, a national convention can be called on proposing this constitutional amendment if 2/3 (34 out of 50 states) of state legislatures apply to Congress to do so. This method was never utilized in U.S. history.

Once this constitutional amendment is passed by Congress, then the next step is ratification, which requires at least 3/4 of the states to ratify this constitutional amendment.

  • 38 out of 50 States are required to ratify

If this Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment (PGPA) is ratified into the United States Constitution, then it would become the 28th Amendment to the United States Constitution (or 29th Amendment if the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) is officially ratified and certified first that it was in legal limbo for decades since expiration). This constitutional amendment would solve democratic and electoral fairness on redrawn congressional or legislative state maps in future elections.

Sponsorship List

I will add a bullet list to credit people here who sponsor or co-sponsor this constitutional amendment. People on this list would mostly be politicians; they could be legislators serving in Congress.

???

NOTE: If you want me to credit you on this list on this constitutional amendment article, then leave a comment on this article that you are sponsoring or co-sponsoring this amendment on eliminating partisan gerrymandering across several states.

  • To be added upon user comments.

Supporters

I will add a bullet list to credit people here who support this constitutional amendment, instead of sponsorship which only applies to politicians. People on this list would mostly be citizens who are not politicians or serving in political office.

NOTE: If you want me to credit you on this list on this constitutional amendment article, then leave a comment on this article that you are supporting this amendment on eliminating partisan gerrymandering across several states.

item.title: The 21st Century Constitutional Reform: 9 Constitutional Amendments For Modern America
item.dc:creator: allenacnguyen
item.content:encoded:
I, Allen Nguyen — an independent citizen from Houston, TX, and a Summa Cum Laude graduate from the University of Houston since May 2025 with a Bachelor of Science in Digital Media — introduce a batch of constitutional amendments that is my tendency to solve 21st-century real-world problems and protesters' grievances in the United States.

  1. 🏥 28th Amendment: Reproductive Freedom Amendment (RFA) [🤰]
  2. 🎓 29th Amendment: Student Digital Liberty Amendment (SDLA) [📱]
  3. ⚙️ 30th Amendment: Labor Stoppage Amendment (LSA) [🛠️]
  4. 🗳️ 31st Amendment: Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment (PGPA) [🗳️]
  5. 💻 32nd Amendment: Artificial Intelligence Regulation Amendment (AIRA) [🤖⚖️]
  6. 📮 33rd Amendment: Postal Delivery Accountability Amendment (PDAA) [📦]
  7. 🛡️ 34th Amendment: Insurance and Financial Security Amendment (IFSA) [💰🛡️]
  8. ⚖️ 35th Amendment: Gender Equality Amendment (GEA) [⚧️⚖️]
  9. 🏛️ 36th Amendment: Campaign Finance Integrity Amendment (CFIA) [💸🛑]

"These are constitutional reforms designed to address real-world problems that existing laws have struggled to solve."

UPDATE 7/7/2026: Added CFIA amendment article.

21st-Century Constitutional Reform Package

🤰 Amendment XXVIII: Reproductive Freedom Amendment (RFA) ↗

Section 1: Fundamental Right to Reproductive Healthcare

Section 1.
