The right of all persons to reproductive freedom — including the right to obtain and access abortion, contraception, fertility treatment (including in vitro fertilization), miscarriage care, prenatal care, childbirth care, and other reproductive healthcare services — shall not be denied, abridged, or infringed by the United States or by any State on account of sex, pregnancy, reproductive status, or the exercise of bodily autonomy.

The exercise of rights protected under this article shall not be restricted, denied, or penalized within any public benefits program, publicly funded healthcare system, or private health insurance plan, nor shall any person be denied emergency care based on institutional or corporate policy.

Subject only to the post-viability provisions set forth in Section 2, the right to reproductive freedom as defined in this Section shall be absolute, and any law, rule, or policy that prohibits, denies, or penalizes its exercise shall be void ab initio. Any administrative, licensing, or facility regulation that indirectly touches upon, delays, or burdens the availability of services protected under this article shall be subject to strict scrutiny upon judicial review, where the defending party must demonstrate a compelling interest achieved through the absolute least restrictive means possible. The protections guaranteed against discrimination and denial of care under this article shall be absolute, and the rights herein shall not be balanced against, diminished by, or subject to exemptions under any federal or state statute, including laws protecting religious, moral, or conscientious objections of corporate, institutional, or employer entities.

Section 2: Fetal Viability Regulation Clause

Section 2. The right to abortion shall be absolute prior to fetal viability, which shall be determined solely by the good-faith professional judgment of the attending licensed healthcare practitioner based on the specific medical facts of the pregnancy. No State shall enact statutory definitions, diagnostic mandates, or evidentiary standards to restrict or influence the practitioner's viability determination, nor shall the designation of 'qualified healthcare practitioner' be narrowed from its standard clinical definition to restrict the scope of available providers. Neither the United States nor any State shall prohibit, impose an undue burden upon, or otherwise interfere with the exercise of such right prior to fetal viability.

After fetal viability, a State may regulate or limit abortion; provided that no law or regulation shall prohibit an abortion when, in the professional judgment of a licensed physician or other qualified healthcare practitioner, the abortion is necessary to preserve the life, physical health, severe and debilitating mental health conditions diagnosed by a qualified licensed professional, or bodily integrity, including conditions that may become life-threatening or cause severe, long-term health complications if treatment is delayed, of the pregnant person.

Physicians and other qualified healthcare practitioners facilitating or dispensing care under this Section shall possess absolute immunity from criminal prosecution, civil liability, or administrative retribution, including the suspension or revocation of professional licensing, by any State or political subdivision.

No State shall impose targeted regulatory, licensing, licensing fees, insurance mandates, or administrative requirements on reproductive healthcare providers, facilities, or patients that are more stringent than those imposed on other outpatient medical practices of similar clinical risk. No State shall modify professional licensing, certification, or scope-of-practice standards; nor shall any State manipulate, delay, artificially backlog, or withhold the administrative processing of professional licenses, institutional certifications, or residency approvals; for the purpose of penalizing, restricting, or discouraging any healthcare practitioner from providing or assisting in care protected under this article.

Section 3: Travel, Distribution, & Interstate Commerce Clause

Section 3. Neither the United States nor any State shall penalize, prosecute, investigate, detain, extradite, or otherwise impose liability upon any person for traveling across State lines, assisting another person in traveling across State lines, or providing, prescribing, dispensing, manufacturing, or distributing lawful reproductive healthcare services by mail, common carrier, telehealth, interactive computer services, or any other means of interstate commerce. Notwithstanding the Extradition Clause of Article IV, Section 2 of this Constitution, no State shall extradite, nor shall the United States compel the extradition of, any person for conduct or travel protected under this article. Full faith and credit shall not be given to any civil or criminal judgment arising from conduct protected under this article.

Section 4: Enhanced Shield, Data Privacy, & Distribution Protection Clause

Section 4. The privacy of all persons in matters concerning reproductive healthcare shall be protected. Neither the United States nor any State shall compel the disclosure, collection, sale, transfer, or use of personal medical, digital, biometric, geolocation, communication, or reproductive health data; nor utilize artificial intelligence, machine learning, or automatic algorithmic systems to infer, predict, or synthesize such data; for the purpose of investigating, penalizing, or restricting the exercise of rights protected by this article. Any data or algorithmic inferences obtained or transferred in violation of this Section, whether voluntarily surrendered or compelled, shall be inadmissible in any criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding. No person, healthcare provider, telecommunications provider, technology company, data broker, or other private actor shall be compelled to participate in the enforcement of laws inconsistent with this article.

No prior or existing federal or state statute, including but not limited to laws regulating the postal service or common carriers, shall be construed or enforced to restrict, prohibit, or penalize the mailing, shipping, or transportation of medications, equipment, medical instruments, devices, information, or supplies used for reproductive healthcare services protected under this article.

Section 5: Enforcement Clause

Section 5. Congress shall have the absolute power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation, including the power to prevent any State or private actor from imposing any burden, restriction, or penalty on the rights protected herein.

Section 6: Immediate Effect Clause

Section 6. This article of amendment shall take effect immediately upon ratification by three-fourths of the States. This article shall be entirely self-executing, immediately operative upon ratification, and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation; and the absence of congressional enforcement legislation shall not be construed to delay, restrict, or deny the immediate judicial enforcement of any right guaranteed herein; notwithstanding any prior statute, executive order, or common-law doctrine to the contrary.

📱 Amendment XXIX: Student Digital Liberty Amendment (SDLA) ↗

Section 1: Student Right to Device Possession and Usage

Section 1. The right of students to possess and use personal digital communication devices within public educational institutions shall not be denied, abridged, or infringed by the United States, any State, any local school board, board of trustees, or any educational authority during designated non-instructional periods — including instructional breaks, free time, meal breaks, and designated periods of rest or wellness. This right shall include the guarantee of unhindered physical access to and personal custody of said devices during these periods.

Section 2: Educator Authority and Academic Accommodations

Section 2. Individual educators, instructional staff, coaches, and school administrators shall retain absolute authority to regulate, limit, or prohibit the use of personal digital communication devices during active instructional time, formal examinations, independent assessments, evaluated artistic or musical performances, sanctioned athletic competitions, laboratory instruction where physical safety mandates strict device control, official school assemblies, mandatory administrative advisory or homeroom periods where announcements are actively delivered, or official school-sponsored activities where such restrictions are strictly necessary to maintain academic integrity, athletic fairness, auditory decorum, or institutional safety. Authorities may mandate that devices be placed completely out of sight, removed from the person, or surrendered to temporary, secure classroom or performance containment during these periods.

Subject to appropriate accommodations for documented medical or educational necessities, individual educators shall retain sole discretion to permit limited instructional device usage within their respective learning environments, including note-taking, photographing instructional materials, or accessing digital learning platforms and real-time academic marks.

Section 3: Safety, Medical, and Privacy Protections

Section 3. No State, school board, district, or educational governing body shall infringe upon a student’s right to possess or use a personal digital communication device for a documented medical necessity, or when a student possesses an objectively reasonable belief — predicated upon observable conditions, audible alarms, or official institutional notification — that an immediate threat to campus security, public safety, or human life exists; including but not limited to active threat scenarios, institutional lockdowns, and severe weather emergencies. The emergency provisions of this section shall supersede any temporary containment policies, and personal custody of such devices shall be restored immediately upon the conclusion of an evaluated performance or upon the triggering of an institutional emergency protocol. The protections herein shall not be infringed, circumvented, or suspended under any administrative, disciplinary, or public safety pretext during non-instructional hours.

Local school boards and governing bodies shall retain the explicit authority to enact reasonable codes of conduct regulating device usage, and shall retain the power to prohibit device usage that violates a reasonable expectation of privacy, including the unauthorized digital recording of individuals in spaces with an inherent expectation of privacy or without explicit consent, constitutes targeted harassment, or actively facilitates or is directly utilized in an ongoing act of academic dishonesty. In communal dining spaces during designated meal periods, authorities may further limit or prohibit live-stream broadcasting, the coordination of unauthorized student gatherings, and the external projection of audio via device loudspeakers to ensure campus security and order; provided, however, that such policies shall regulate student conduct rather than impose total prohibition during the school day. No State, school board, or educational authority shall intentionally jam, degrade, or disrupt cellular signals or digital networks within educational facilities as a mechanism to restrict device usage, nor mandate the installation of monitoring software on personal devices as a condition of campus access, nor intentionally employ digital routing, domain filtering, or architectural shielding during non-instructional periods to circumvent the intent of this article.

Section 4: Definitions and Construction

Section 4. For the purposes of this article, "personal digital communication device" shall mean any handheld cellular telephone, wearable smart timepiece, tablet computer, or successor mobile electronic hardware engineered primarily for individual wireless communication, data retrieval, or personal computing, owned or legally possessed by the individual student. This article shall not be construed to protect the use of non-communicative electronic entertainment systems or any technology or manner of device usage, including un-buffered external audio broadcast, that inherently disrupts the institutional environment or undermines campus safety.

"Non-instructional periods" shall be construed as any block of time exceeding ten consecutive minutes where active classroom instruction, formal examination, sanctioned athletic competition, or evaluated artistic performance is not actively occurring — including standard lunch breaks, passing periods, and study halls — regardless of whether an educational authority reclassifies or renames such blocks as mandatory non-curriculum activities, subject to the institutional conduct and privacy restrictions set forth in Section 3 of this article. During designated passing periods, the possession of personal digital communication devices remains protected; however, local educational authorities may regulate device usage only where it creates an imminent, severe physical safety hazard or a complete blockage of transit hallways, provided that the non-disruptive handling of or brief glances at a device for timekeeping, schedule verification, or personal communication remain unabridged and shall not prima facie constitute a safety hazard.

Section 5: Enforcement Clause

Section 5. Congress shall have the power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation, including the authority to condition federal educational funding upon strict compliance with the provisions herein, and to establish administrative remedies for the administrative or systemic deprivation of the rights guaranteed by this article.

Section 6: Immediate Effect Clause

Section 6. This article of amendment shall take effect immediately upon ratification by three-fourths of the States. This article shall be entirely self-executing, immediately operative upon ratification, and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation; and the absence of congressional enforcement legislation shall not be construed to delay, restrict, or deny the immediate judicial enforcement of any right guaranteed herein; notwithstanding any prior statute, executive order, or common-law doctrine to the contrary.

🛠️ Amendment XXX: Labor Stoppage Amendment (LSA) ↗

Section 1: The Right to Work Stoppage

Section 1.

1–1: Employee Right to Work Stoppage. The right of employees in both the public and private sectors to engage in strikes, work stoppages, or other collective labor actions in connection with labor disputes — including disputes over compensation, insurance, benefits, staffing levels, workplace safety, and terms or conditions of employment — shall not be denied, abridged, or infringed by the United States or any State.

1–2: Employer Right to Lockout, Limitations on Lockouts, and Private Sector Insolvency Exemption. Employers and their designated executives in both the public and private sectors shall retain the right to impose lockouts during labor disputes; provided that such lockouts do not exceed a cumulative total of fourteen calendar days per dispute, do not result in the permanent replacement or termination of employees, do not disrupt essential or critical services as defined or regulated under Sections 3 and 4, and do not infringe upon the benefit and seniority protections guaranteed herein. On the fifteenth calendar day of an active lockout, or upon any lockout enacted in bad faith to deplete union resources without active collective bargaining, such action shall be explicitly deemed an unlawful economic penalty and a constructive termination. This milestone shall trigger immediate full backpay liabilities for the employer and the instant suspension of all employee non-compete covenants for the remaining duration of the dispute; except that in the private sector, an employer may petition a court of competent jurisdiction for a temporary extension of a lockout solely upon a clear and convincing showing of extreme operational insolvency that threatens the permanent cessation of all business operations; provided that such insolvency must be demonstrated across the consolidated financial structure of the employer's entire corporate enterprise, including all parent companies, domestic or international subsidiaries, holding companies, and controlled affiliates.

1–3: Non-Forfeiture of Accrued Vested Benefits and Anti-Retaliation Protection. No person shall suffer the forfeiture, reduction, suspension, or adverse recalculation of pension or retirement benefits, nor the suspension, termination, or reduction of employer contributions toward health, life, disability, or other welfare insurance plans, nor any loss of accrued seniority, service-credit hours, re-employment rights, or any other penalty or retaliation for participating in such labor actions. All retirement benefits and credits accrued prior to or during a protected labor action shall be deemed unalterable, vested property of the employee. No employee shall be permanently replaced, terminated, subjected to economic layoff, or otherwise economically penalized for participating in a protected labor action.

1–4: Prohibitions on Labor Substitutions, Military Interventions, and Algorithmic Strikebreaking

Subsection 1–4(a): Prohibition on Human Personnel Substitution. During a protected labor action or any period where work is withheld due to a failure of timely compensation, no employer, nor any official of the United States or any State, shall temporarily or permanently replace, substitute, or supplement the striking personnel to perform the operational, specialized, security, management, or administrative functions historically performed by the affected bargaining unit.

Subsection 1–4(b): Restrictions on External Workforces, Funding Status, and National Guard Deployment. The prohibition established in subsection (a) shall explicitly apply to the deployment of personnel from other agencies, departments, sub-agencies, or external workforces; private third-party independent contractors; temporary staffing agencies; or any corporate parent, subsidiary, or affiliated division. No officer of the United States, any State, or any political subdivision thereof shall evade the protections of this article through the temporary reassignment, detail, deputization, cross-designation, emergency designation, or interagency transfer of personnel to perform duties historically performed by the affected bargaining unit. This prohibition further bars any internal non-bargaining unit employees, salaried managers, corporate executives, or workers from unaffected internal divisions performing functions outside their historical daily duties — as well as the emergency deployment, or increased operational utilization and scaling, of automated systems, generative software, and artificial intelligence designed to mimic or replace human labor functions historically performed by the bargaining unit. The National Guard and military reserves may be deployed to perform bargaining unit functions solely and exclusively upon a binding judicial declaration that such deployment is the single available means to avert an instantaneous, catastrophic threat to human life or public health; provided, however, that such deployment shall be strictly limited to the execution of core life-saving or environmental safety functions, shall never extend to administrative, logistical, or standard operational duties, and shall immediately terminate upon the cessation of the acute life threat — regardless of whether such substituting personnel belong to an agency that remains funded or possesses alternative federal, state, or statutory authority during a partial or total government shutdown.

Subsection 1–4(c): Absolute Ceilings on Automated Workflows and Digital Strikebreaking. The prohibitions established across the entirety of this Section shall further apply to the direct or indirect procurement or activation of automated workflows, third-party software-as-a-service, or algorithmically driven external platforms intended to offset or absorb the operational deficit caused by the labor action. Under no circumstances shall any pre-existing automated system, algorithmic process, artificial intelligence framework, software platform, or digital workflow be permitted to increase its operational output, workload capacity, task volume, autonomous execution, transaction throughput, decision-making authority, or functional utilization beyond the average daily parameters recorded during the ninety calendar days immediately preceding the commencement of the labor action, or during the corresponding seasonal calendar period in the preceding fiscal year, whichever baseline reflects a lower threshold of automated throughput. Any operational reliance on such systems that bypasses or substitutes for the historical human verification, modification, or supervision of the striking bargaining unit shall constitute a per se violation of this Section.

Section 2: Enforcement Clause

Section 2. Congress shall have the power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation, including the establishment of procedures, protections, and remedies necessary to implement the rights set forth herein. Notwithstanding this enforcement power, the provisions of Section 1 of this article shall be self-executing and shall take effect regardless of the enactment of implementing legislation.

Section 3: Essential Services Work Stoppage Restrictions

Section 3.

3–1: Categorization of Essential Services and Congressional Oversight. The rights guaranteed by Section 1 of this article shall not extend to labor actions within essential services where a temporary work stoppage would pose an immediate, direct, and severe threat to public safety, national defense, or national security. For purposes of this article, essential services shall be strictly limited to law enforcement, firefighting services, emergency medical personnel, air traffic controllers, aviation security personnel, members of the armed forces, and the direct operational, cybersecurity, and digital infrastructure personnel required to maintain the continuous functioning of nuclear, electrical, water treatment, and natural gas utility systems. Congress shall retain the authority to regulate labor actions by employees in these designated essential services and members of the armed forces to protect national defense, national security, and the public welfare.

3–2: Automatic Dissolution of Strike Restrictions Upon Compensation Default. Notwithstanding such classifications, any restriction on labor actions under this section shall immediately dissolve, and the full right to engage in strikes, work stoppages, or the withholding of labor protected under Section 1 shall be restored, if the employing public or private entity fails to provide timely, scheduled compensation in full on the established date of payroll. For the purposes of this article, a failure to deliver full compensation within forty-eight hours of the calendar day on which payroll is contractually or statutorily due shall constitute an absolute default; provided, however, that this window shall extend to seventy-two hours solely in verified events of systemic, third-party banking infrastructure failure or widespread digital network outages independent of the employer's control; provided further that the employer has otherwise initiated and fully funded the payroll obligation. Under no circumstances shall a lapse in legislative appropriations, a government shutdown, or an employer's internal administrative error qualify for said seventy-two-hour extension. For the purposes of this article, a lapse in federal, state, or municipal appropriations, resulting in a government shutdown, the temporary suspension of agency funding, or the imposition of mandatory unpaid furloughs, shall constitute a per se failure to provide timely, scheduled compensation, and no affected employee shall be compelled to perform labor without contemporaneous, full fiscal compensation.

3–3: Strict Construction of Essential Personnel Duties and Protection of Auxiliary Roles. For the purposes of this Section, the classification of 'essential services' shall be strictly construed based on the specific, real-time duties performed by the employee, rather than job titles, civil service rankings, or broad agency designations. Classification under this Section shall require a showing that the specific employee's immediate absence creates a direct, un-attenuated threat of physical destruction or loss of life, independent of general economic or operational inconvenience. The inclusion of digital infrastructure and cybersecurity personnel shall apply solely to those individuals whose immediate, un-substituted absence would cause an instantaneous and catastrophic failure of utility grids, water sanitation, or nuclear safety systems; wherein such failure would result in immediate bodily harm, loss of life, or widespread biological contamination. Under no circumstances shall this classification be expanded by the United States, any State, or political subdivision thereof to encompass general administrative, technical support, educational, or auxiliary public sector roles.

Section 4: Critical Infrastructure & Supply Chain Mandates

Section 4.

4–1: Minimum Operational Mandates for Supply Chain Preservation. Congress shall have the authority to require that employees in critical transport, logistics, maritime ports, freight rail, commercial aviation, and infrastructure sectors maintain minimum operations during a labor dispute solely to prevent an imminent threat to public safety or a catastrophic collapse of the national supply chain vital to human survival; provided, however, that during any active labor action affecting these sectors, all participating entities shall preserve the continuous, safety-compliant handling, temperature-monitoring, pressure-relief regulation, and atmospheric ventilation of cryogenic refrigerants, hazardous cooling agents, volatile chemical assets, Class 9 lithium-ion battery systems, and critical petroleum products — including but not limited to solid carbon dioxide (UN1845/dry ice), refrigerated liquid nitrogen (UN1977), Class 2.3 toxic inhalation gases, Class 5.2 thermally unstable organic peroxides, Class 9 lithium-ion cell configurations (UN3480/UN3481), Class 3 bulk refined petroleum or aviation fuels, high-amperage industrial electrical couplers, critical fleet transport or heavy manufacturing components, and any analogous hazardous materials, volatile chemical assets, or advanced energy storage technologies classified under current or subsequent federal or international transit safety standards — to prevent cargo degradation, explosive atmospheric decomposition, pressure-induced package rupture, regional energy grid starvation, thermal runaway propagation, widespread electrical infrastructure disconnection, systemic vehicle fleet depletion, or crew asphyxiation in confined transit compartments.

4–2: Funding Pre-Requisites for Minimum Mandates and Emergency Appropriations. However, if a labor action in these sectors is triggered by an employer’s default on timely, scheduled payroll, Congress may invoke a minimum operational mandate only if it simultaneously guarantees full, immediate payment of all affected personnel through emergency appropriations. Absent the enactment and fulfillment of such immediate funding, all operational mandates and restrictions on work stoppages under this Section shall dissolve, and the full protections and rights established in Section 1 shall apply without qualification.

Section 5: Immunity from Civil Liability and Injunctions

Section 5.

5–1: Complete Shield from Tort Liabilities and Restrictions on Judicial Injunctions. No labor organization, collective bargaining unit, or individual officer or member thereof shall be held civilly liable in any court of the United States or any State for economic damages, lost profits, or business disruption resulting from a protected labor action under this article. No court of the United States or any State shall have jurisdiction to issue temporary restraining orders, preliminary injunctions, or permanent injunctions to halt, delay, or restrict any labor action protected under Section 1, except upon a clear showing of imminent, physical violence directly perpetrated by striking personnel causing immediate bodily injury or active property destruction. The manifestation of widespread economic disruption, operational delays, financial losses, supply chain friction, or structural budgetary deficits shall never be construed by any court as constituting physical violence, public danger, or a constructive threat to physical safety under this Section.

5–2: Corporate and Successor Accountability, Anti-Retaliation Presumptions, and Mandatory Judicial Status Quo Orders. The prohibitions under this Section shall bind the employer without limitation, including any parent corporations, domestic or international subsidiaries, shell companies, contracted third-party entities, or automated technological frameworks and artificial intelligence systems operating to substitute for the duties of the affected workforce. Furthermore, any mass layoff, departmental elimination, discretionary elimination of program funding, targeted legislative defunding of specific bargaining units, or selective workforce reduction initiated by an employer or by a legislative or governing body during an active labor dispute or within ninety days of its resolution shall carry a rebuttable presumption of unlawful labor retaliation, regardless of whether such actions are attributed to a power grid failure, natural disaster, or other emergency pretext. Courts of the United States or any State shall have jurisdiction and a mandatory constitutional obligation to issue immediate interim injunctive relief to freeze such layoffs or funding cuts pending the final adjudication of a full administrative audit of the employer's financial necessity. The core fact-finding and administrative audit shall be executed by a designated federal or state labor regulatory agency, or an independent special master appointed by the court, the preliminary phase of which must be concluded within thirty calendar days of filing; provided that the court finds sufficient cause to continue the interim freeze; and provided further that the final audit must be fully adjudicated within ninety calendar days, during which time all affected employees shall remain fully employed with undisturbed compensation and benefits.

Section 6: Effect Delay Clause

Section 6. This article of amendment shall take effect six months after the date of ratification, providing states, employers, and employees adequate time to adjust to the rights and obligations established herein. Upon the date of ratification and during this interim period, no employer or State shall take any retaliatory or adverse employment action against employees, nor execute layoffs, nor alter pension, insurance, or re-employment rights, in anticipation of the protections established herein. This article shall be entirely self-executing, with its interim anti-retaliation protections becoming immediately operative upon ratification, and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation, safeguarding all accrued pensions, insurance plans, and benefits under an absolute constitutional firewall that shall remain non-waivable during any fiscal crisis or emergency pretext. This absolute constitutional firewall safeguards all accrued pensions, insurance plans, and benefits, and it shall remain non-waivable during any fiscal crisis or emergency pretext.

🗳️ Amendment XXXI: Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment (PGPA) ↗

Section 1: Prohibition of the Intent of Partisan Gerrymandering

Section 1. All legislative bodies covered under this article shall be elected exclusively from single-member geographic districts, unless an alternative proportional representation framework is explicitly authorized by Congress. Districts established for the election of Members of the United States House of Representatives, members of the lower chamber of any State legislature, and members of the upper chamber of any State legislature, shall not be drawn, altered, or maintained for the purpose of favoring or disadvantaging a political party, its candidates, or any coalition of voters or supporters based on shared political alignment.

Section 2: Prohibition of the Outcome of Undue Partisan Advantage

Section 2. No State, political subdivision, officer, commission, legislature, or other governmental authority shall enact, approve, or implement any congressional, State House, or State Senate redistricting plan that has the purpose or effect of granting an undue partisan advantage, as defined in Section 5 of this article, or disadvantage to any political party or to any group of citizens based on their voting history or political alignment.

Section 3: Judicial Review, Remedies, and Evidence Clause

Section 3. Any redistricting plan for the United States House of Representatives, a State House of Representatives or equivalent lower legislative chamber, or a State Senate or equivalent upper legislative chamber shall be subject to judicial review. Federal and State courts shall have authority to determine whether a plan complies with this article and to provide appropriate remedies, including the invalidation of unlawful districts and the adoption or supervision of lawful replacement plans; provided that any judicially adopted map must maximize mathematical neutrality, minimize measurable partisan asymmetry, satisfy all applicable constitutional requirements, and perform no worse than the median of independently generated neutral ensemble maps according to the standards established by this article over all rejected alternatives. In determining compliance, courts may consider statistical evidence, mathematical modeling, algorithmic simulations, artificial intelligence modeling, machine learning analysis, ensemble map analyses, historical patterns, expert analysis, computational modeling, transparent and independently reproducible algorithmic methods, peer-reviewed methodologies where reasonably practicable, and any other relevant indicators of partisan bias or mathematical neutrality.

Section 4: Neutral Standards and Counting Clause

Section 4. In reviewing redistricting plans, courts shall apply neutral and objective standards consistent with constitutional fairness. The primary criteria for compliance shall be electoral fairness, the minimization of partisan bias, and the proportionality of seats to votes as measured across a range of reasonable electoral outcomes, with mathematical neutrality as defined in Section 5 of this article. The criteria of electoral fairness and mathematical proportionality of seats to votes shall constitute the highest constitutional standards governing the review of districting plans. Where geographic compactness, contiguity, or respect for political subdivisions conflict with or produce a statistically significant deviation from mathematical proportionality, such traditional criteria must yield to ensure proportional fairness. Consistent with these primary criteria, courts may consider geographic compactness, contiguity, respect for political subdivisions, and respect for communities of interest. Any map layout resulting in a deviation from mathematical proportionality or partisan symmetry that exceeds two standard deviations from the mean of the distribution of constitutionally compliant electoral outcomes generated through independently verified, transparent, and non-partisan neutral ensemble modeling, as defined in Section 5 of this article, shall be unconstitutional, thereby leaving courts with no discretionary authority to validate maps displaying artificial partisan asymmetry measured across a historically grounded range of statewide electoral outcomes. Any artificial intelligence system, machine learning model, computational algorithm, or statistical methodology relied upon under this article shall be publicly disclosed, independently reproducible, auditable, and subject to adversarial examination by all parties before judicial consideration.

For the purposes of establishing population equality under this article, incarcerated individuals shall be counted at their last known legal residence prior to incarceration. Where a prior legal residence cannot be verified after an exhaustive, judicially verifiable audit, the individual shall be apportioned uniformly across all state districts entirely, rather than counted at the facility of incarceration; ensuring that under no circumstances or administrative default shall any such individual be counted or assigned to the population base of the political subdivision containing the facility of incarceration.

Section 5: Definitions

Section 5. For the purposes of this article:

'Mathematical neutrality' means the absence of statistically significant partisan asymmetry relative to the distribution of outcomes produced through independently verified neutral ensemble modeling.

'Neutral ensemble modeling' means the generation of a sufficiently large collection of constitutionally compliant districting plans through transparent, reproducible, non-partisan computational methods without regard to the expected electoral performance of any political party.

'Undue partisan advantage' means a statistically significant deviation from mathematical neutrality that cannot reasonably be explained by geography, constitutional requirements, or random variation.

Section 6: Enforcement Clause

Section 6. Congress shall have power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation. Such legislation may establish minimum national standards for congressional and State legislative redistricting, may regulate or prohibit the use of proprietary artificial intelligence technologies, machine learning systems, computational optimization algorithms, and substantially equivalent future technologies designed to optimize partisan advantage, and may authorize, require, or regulate independent redistricting commissions for the establishment of districts for the United States House of Representatives, State Houses of Representatives or equivalent lower legislative chambers, and State Senates or equivalent upper legislative chambers. Any independent redistricting commission authorized or required under this article shall be guaranteed non-discretionary public funding sufficient to fulfill its duties, and the selection process for its members shall be fully transparent, verifiable, and subject to expedited judicial review to prevent partisan capture.

Congress may require that all computational models, artificial intelligence systems, statistical software, source code where practicable, datasets, assumptions, and ensemble generation methodologies used in official redistricting be publicly documented and independently verifiable. All datasets, software, computational methods, assumptions, statistical analyses, and ensemble generation methodologies relied upon pursuant to this article shall be subject to public disclosure and independent inspection, except where nondisclosure is required by this Constitution or by other provisions of law enacted pursuant thereto.

Section 7: Effective Date & Frequency Clause

Section 7. This article shall take effect immediately upon ratification and shall immediately invalidate any non-compliant maps then in effect, regardless of when they were enacted, and shall apply to all districts for the United States House of Representatives, State Houses of Representatives or equivalent lower legislative chambers, and State Senates or equivalent upper legislative chambers thereafter. Districts covered under this article shall be established no more than once per decennial census cycle, except when strictly required by a court of competent jurisdiction to remedy a violation of law. This article shall be entirely self-executing and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation.

🤖⚖️ Amendment XXXII: Artificial Intelligence Regulation Amendment (AIRA) ↗

Section 1: Purpose and Scope of Artificial Intelligence

Section 1.

1–1: Scope of Governance. Artificial intelligence (AI), including autonomous systems, generative models, robotics, and digital agents, shall be governed to protect the rights, safety, and dignity of all persons when such systems are deployed in a manner that materially affects legal rights, access to essential services, or significant personal or governmental decision-making by directly determining eligibility, approval, denial, ranking, sentencing, or materially dispositive outcomes affecting such rights or services, or by substantially influencing outcomes where a reasonable observer would conclude that the artificial intelligence system functions as a determinative or presumptively controlling factor in the decision-making process.

1–2: Functional Impact and Technological Neutrality. For purposes of this article, material effect shall be determined by the functional impact of the system on outcomes affecting legal rights, access to essential services, or governmental decision-making, rather than by the technical design or labeling of the system. Artificial intelligence usage shall be subject to constitutional safeguards that are technologically neutral and applicable to substantially equivalent computational systems regardless of architecture, methodology, or nomenclature to prevent misuse, fraudulent or deceptive conduct attributable to such systems, and harmful outcomes arising from their deployment in governmental functions or private activities materially affecting legal rights, essential services, or public welfare.

Section 2: Rights of Citizens

Section 2.

2–1: Right to Transparency. Every person shall enjoy the right to prompt and conspicuous disclosure whenever an artificial intelligence system fundamentally influences decisions determining their legal rights, liberties, or access to essential public opportunities including employment, housing, credit, education, healthcare, insurance, law enforcement action, or governmental benefits. Disclosure shall include notice of artificial intelligence involvement and the general category of decision-making influence, as defined by Congress. Such disclosure shall include, to the extent reasonably practicable and consistent with legitimate security, privacy, and proprietary interests, a plain-language explanation sufficient to permit a reasonable person to understand the principal factors materially contributing to the determination.

2–2: Requirement of Human Review. No final determination depriving a person of life, liberty, property, or fundamental rights shall be executed solely by algorithmic or automated means without independent and meaningful human review occurring prior to the final effectuation of such decision. Such review shall include independent authority to override, modify, reverse, or reject the automated determination based on a substantive review of underlying facts, evidence, and reasoning; such authority shall be final with respect to the administrative effectuation of the determination.

2–3: Standards for Meaningful Oversight. Human review shall not be satisfied by automated approval workflows, or predetermined or mechanically affirmed decisions; it shall require access to the material data inputs, outputs, documentation, and explanatory records reasonably necessary to evaluate the basis of the determination. Any human reviewer exercising authority under this Section shall possess sufficient authority, independence, and access to relevant information to conduct a meaningful and impartial evaluation of the determination. Such review shall not be satisfied by predetermined approval protocols, automated escalation filters lacking substantive discretion, or organizational structures designed to predetermine the outcome of review.

2–4: Emergency Exceptions. Congress may provide narrowly tailored emergency exceptions, applicable only to individualized determinations, where immediate action is necessary to prevent a specific, imminent, and demonstrable risk of death or serious physical injury to an identifiable person or group — provided that the invocation of such exemption is verified by a human officer, any determination executed pursuant to such emergency circumstances shall be subject to prompt post-deprivation review, and such exceptions shall not extend to generalized, statistical, or system-level risk assessments.

Section 3: Standards for AI Safety and Accountability

Section 3.

3–1: Liability & Accountability. Civil and criminal liability for actions, outputs, or damages caused by an artificial intelligence system or the autonomous physical actions of any vehicle or machinery guided thereby shall be attributed to the human or legal entity that deploys, operates, or materially controls such system in the context of its use; an autonomous system shall not be recognized as a legal person capable of bearing liability. Congress may define tiers of responsibility among developers, deployers, operators, owners, and users based upon degree of control, foreseeability, knowledge, and material contribution to the harm.

3–2: Preservation of Product Liability and Anti-Evasion. No developer, deployer, operator, owner, distributor, or materially participating entity shall evade liability through contractual delegation, indemnification agreements, corporate restructuring, or the transfer of operational control after deployment, nor shall the utilization of artificial intelligence in the design, testing, or manufacturing of a product diminish the strict product liability of its producers or distributors for defects resulting therefrom. Nothing herein shall prohibit Congress from imposing joint and several liability upon multiple responsible parties whose conduct materially contributed to the harm. Nothing in this article shall be construed to exempt governmental entities from liability, remedies, or judicial review otherwise authorized by law.

3–3: Financial Assurances and Mandatory Insurance. Congress shall possess the authority to require entities deploying autonomous or high-risk artificial intelligence systems to maintain adequate liability insurance or certified financial assurances sufficient to satisfy potential claims arising under this article.

3–4: Certification. Congress shall possess the authority to mandate rigorous safety standards and public certifications for high-risk autonomous systems defined as systems whose outputs directly affect legal rights, essential services, physical safety, or designated critical infrastructure systems designated by Congress through publicly enacted legislation and subject to periodic review deployed in commerce, government, or critical infrastructure prior to their introduction into public commerce.

Section 4: Ethical and Responsible Use

Section 4.

4–1: Prohibition of Malicious Use. The knowing utilization of artificial intelligence to perpetrate fraud, facilitate criminal impersonation, materially deceive persons in a manner causing legally cognizable harm, engage in systemic subversion of democratic processes through covert foreign state-sponsored operations or verified widespread voter deception, or facilitate the non-consensual weaponized impersonation of individuals is strictly prohibited.

4–2: Standard for Deceptive Conduct. For the purposes of this article, conduct shall be deemed deceptive when a reasonable person acting under the circumstances of distribution would foresee that the output generated by an artificial intelligence system is materially likely to mislead a reasonable person acting under similar informational conditions in the relevant medium of distribution, including political, commercial, journalistic, or private interpersonal contexts, and when the content is presented or reasonably understood under the circumstances of distribution to be human-authored or authentic human expression without adequate disclosure of artificial generation as to authorship, identity, or factual authenticity. Clearly labeled parody, satire, artistic expression, or fictional content shall not constitute deception under this Section.

4–3: Protection Against Bias. Artificial intelligence systems deployed by or on behalf of any government entity shall be designed and audited in accordance with publicly established, non-discriminatory technical standards defined by Congress or independent regulatory authority to ensure that their design, deployment, and operation do not intentionally deny or abridge equal protection under the law or produce unlawful discrimination prohibited by law. Any audit required under this article shall be conducted by an independent and professionally qualified entity possessing no direct financial interest in, ownership stake in, managerial authority over, or contractual dependency upon the system subject to audit.

4–4: Human Primacy. Artificial intelligence systems shall remain subject to identifiable human decision-making authority and ultimate human accountability whenever deployed in governmental functions or in any determination materially affecting constitutional rights, legal status, or access to essential public services. For the purposes of this Section, no artificial intelligence system shall possess independent constitutional rights, legal personhood, or authority to exercise sovereign governmental powers, except where expressly authorized by law, consistent with this Constitution, and subject at all times to meaningful human supervision and accountability, which shall remain exclusively exercised by constitutionally accountable human officers and shall not be delegated to artificial intelligence systems in whole or in part.

Section 5: Governance of Synthetic Media and Digital Likeness

Section 5.

5–1: Right to Create & Fair Use. The right of the people to generate synthetic imagery and video for lawful expressive, artistic, journalistic, and educational purposes shall not be infringed, subject to reasonable restrictions against fraud and targeted harm. This right shall not be construed to supersede the protections of Section 6 concerning voice, likeness, or personal persona. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to abridge constitutionally protected speech, including commentary, criticism, parody, satire, artistic expression, journalism, academic inquiry, or transformative works, except where such expression constitutes unlawful fraud or materially deceptive impersonation causing legally cognizable harm.

5–2: Prohibition of Deceptive Use, Disclosure, and Harm. The distribution of synthetically generated or altered visual media, including deepfake video, that depicts historical or current events with the intent to deceive the public, fabricate legal evidence, or inflict severe emotional distress through non-consensual explicit depictions is prohibited when such content is presented in a manner that creates a material risk of public deception or harm, including impersonation in political, financial, electoral, governmental, or legal contexts. Congress may require conspicuous disclosure of materially altered synthetic political communications distributed to the public during the period beginning ninety days before and ending on the date of a federal election, unless Congress prescribes a different period.

Section 6: Sovereignty of Voice and Likeness

Section 6.

6–1: Inherent Property Right. Every person possesses a protected and exclusive legal interest in their natural voice, visual likeness, and personal persona against any commercial exploitation, deceptive use, or materially misleading synthetic reproduction without explicit consent, including political advertising, endorsement, fundraising communications, and monetized digital replication, which shall extend to the person's estate for no less than a minimum period prescribed by Congress following their death; provided, however, that such right shall remain subject to limitations for matters of public concern, historical record, journalism, and constitutionally protected speech.

6–2: Prohibition of Unauthorized Replication. The unauthorized, deceptive replication or public distribution of a person’s synthetic voice or likeness is prohibited, except where such use constitutes protected commentary, parody, or news reporting, and does not create a likelihood of false endorsement or factual fabrication as determined by a reasonable consumer standard in commercial or political contexts. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to prohibit the use of a person’s likeness or voice for bona fide historical, academic, biographical, or documentary purposes; provided such use does not falsely imply endorsement or fabricate events.

6–3: Freedom of Consent. No person shall be bound by digital likeness licensing agreements lacking explicit, informed, unbundled, and revocable consent. Consent for the use of voice, likeness, or digital persona shall not be inferred from general terms-of-service agreements or bundled contracts — it must be obtained through clear, separate, and affirmative authorization; provided, that Congress may define standardized consent frameworks for limited commercial licensing agreements.

6–4: Protection of Data and Identity. Congress shall have the authority to establish reasonable safeguards governing the collection, retention, use, and commercial exploitation of personal data by artificial intelligence systems where necessary to protect privacy, identity, property, or individual autonomy consistent with this Constitution. Such safeguards shall be narrowly tailored to legitimate privacy and identity-protection interests and shall not be construed to prohibit lawful scientific research, security testing, or public-interest data analysis conducted in accordance with applicable law.

Section 7: Governance and Oversight

Section 7.

7–1: Regulatory Framework and Suspension Power. Congress shall provide for independent oversight of advanced artificial intelligence systems through such authority, agency, commission, or regulatory framework as it may establish by law. Such authority shall possess the power to temporarily suspend or isolate specific components of systems presenting a clear, demonstrable, imminent, and catastrophic threat to public safety, national security, or constitutional order via the most narrowly tailored means available where less restrictive regulatory measures are insufficient to mitigate such threat.

7–2: Evidentiary Standards and Judicial Review. No suspension shall issue absent documented findings supported by clear and convincing evidence. Such findings shall be subject to prompt judicial review, and the evidentiary standard shall be evaluated de novo by the reviewing court. For the purposes of this article, a “clear, demonstrable, imminent, and catastrophic threat” shall mean a demonstrable and immediate risk of mass casualty, catastrophic infrastructure failure, or large-scale disruption of democratic governance. Congress shall receive prompt notice of any suspension issued under this Section and may prescribe additional procedures for oversight and review.

7–3: Due Process and Judicial Review. No suspension under this Section shall be used to override or nullify individual due process rights guaranteed under Section 2 — except where such suspension is itself necessary to prevent imminent catastrophic harm as defined herein. Any suspension shall be subject to prompt judicial review within a period prescribed by Congress, which shall not unreasonably delay judicial consideration of the suspension.

7–4: Limitations and Institutional Integrity. No suspension under this Section shall exceed the minimum duration necessary to mitigate the identified threat; it shall automatically terminate upon cessation of such threat unless renewed by a separate judicial determination. The governing structure of such authority shall provide institutional independence, transparency, public reporting, and protections against direct partisan control as defined by Congress.

Section 8: Sovereignty and Security of AI Infrastructure

Section 8.

8–1: Infrastructure Classification and Grid Resilience. Advanced artificial intelligence data centers, hyperscale computing facilities, and the primary physical infrastructure underpinning high-risk automated systems are recognized as strategic national utilities vital to public infrastructure and national security. No human or legal entity shall construct, expand, or operate such facilities in a manner that compromises the stability, reliability, or baseline capacity of local or national electrical grids, nor shall the energy demands of such facilities disproportionately shift utility costs onto residential consumers.

8–2: Environmental and Resource Guardrails. The operation of advanced computing infrastructure shall remain subject to strict public accountability regarding natural resource consumption. Congress and the several States shall retain the authority to regulate, limit, or condition the extraction of public water resources and the utilization of fossil-fuel power generation by data center facilities to prevent localized ecological degradation, systemic environmental harm, or the subversion of state and local resource management.

8–3: Physical Security and Sovereign Continuity. As critical infrastructure, hyperscale data centers hosting advanced artificial intelligence systems shall be hardened against physical, kinetic, and digital threats to ensure sovereign operational continuity. The ownership, material control, or structural leasing of critical computing infrastructure within the United States by prohibited foreign adversaries or their proxies is strictly prohibited.

Section 9: Innovation and Public Benefit

Section 9. Congress and the States shall possess the authority to incentivize and promote the development of artificial intelligence systems designed to advance the public welfare and common defense. Safety standards and best practices shall be publicly accessible. This article shall be construed in a technologically neutral manner and shall apply to future computational systems performing substantially equivalent functions to those regulated herein. Nothing in this article shall be construed to prohibit lawful scientific research, open scientific publication, security research, testing, or academic inquiry conducted in accordance with applicable law.

Section 10: Definitions

Section 10.

10–1: Definition of Artificial Intelligence. ‘Artificial intelligence’ refers to computational systems that generate predictions, classifications, recommendations, decisions, or content through machine-learned, adaptive, inferential, probabilistic, or substantially equivalent computational processes, including systems that functionally replicate such capabilities regardless of underlying architecture, methodology, or implementation.

10–2: Definition of AI-Generated Imagery and Video. ‘AI‑generated imagery and video’ includes photorealistic, synthetic, or materially altered visual content, moving images, or cinematographic sequences produced or modified by artificial intelligence, including depictions that a reasonable observer could mistake for authentic recordings.

10–3: Definition of Deepfake Video. ‘Deepfake video’ refers to synthetically generated or altered digital video recordings that realistically depict a person’s likeness, actions, or speech occurring in a manner that did not actually transpire, produced with the intent or effect of appearing authentic to a reasonable observer.

10–4: Definition of AI-Generated Voice. 'AI-generated voice' refers to synthetic audio replicating or imitating a natural human voice.

10–5: Definition of Likeness. 'Likeness' includes the unique visual, auditory, or behavioral characteristics identifying a specific individual.

10–6: Definition of Autonomous System. ‘Autonomous system’ refers to any machine, software, or computational process capable of operating without continuous human direction in a manner that materially affects human rights, property, or public infrastructure.

10–7: Definition of Digital Persona. ‘Digital persona’ refers to the composite of a person’s identifiable characteristics, including voice, likeness, mannerisms, behavioral patterns, or other attributes that enable recognition in digital or synthetic media when such use is intended to represent a specific identifiable individual.

Section 11: Anti-Evasion Clause

Section 11. Neither the United States nor any State, nor any public or private actor subject to this article, shall evade the protections or restrictions herein through contractual arrangements, technological intermediaries, nominal human oversight, corporate restructuring, geographic displacement, or through any substantially equivalent mechanism, arrangement, designation, intermediary, or technological process whose practical effect is to circumvent the protections or obligations established by this article, whether formally designated as artificial intelligence or described by any other technological classification. The protections and obligations of this article shall not be avoided through foreign outsourcing, intermediary entities, subcontracting arrangements, or materially equivalent operational structures.

Section 12: Severability Clause

Section 12. If any provision of this article, or the application thereof, is held invalid, the remainder of the article and its application to other persons or circumstances shall remain in full force and effect to the maximum extent constitutionally permissible.

Section 13: Enforcement Clause

Section 13.

13–1: Legislative Enforcement Power. Congress shall have the power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation, including civil penalties, administrative enforcement mechanisms, and judicially reviewable regulatory standards consistent with this article.

13–2: Due Process Balance. In the event of conflict between emergency suspension powers under Section 7 and individual rights under Section 2, courts shall apply the least restrictive interpretation necessary to preserve constitutional due process consistent with imminent catastrophic risk prevention.

13–3: Standing and Equitable Remedies. Any person suffering a concrete, particularized, or legally cognizable injury arising from a violation of this article shall have standing to seek injunctive relief, declaratory relief, and damages where authorized by law, upon showing that the artificial intelligence system or its deployment was a substantial and proximate factor in the injury, without requirement of showing exclusive causation, and shall be entitled to such additional equitable relief as necessary to fully remedy the violation.

Section 14: Immediate Effect Clause

Section 14. This article of amendment shall take effect immediately upon ratification by three-fourths of the States. This article shall be entirely self-executing, immediately operative upon ratification, and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation; and the absence of congressional enforcement legislation shall not be construed to delay, restrict, or deny the immediate judicial enforcement of any right guaranteed herein; notwithstanding any prior statute, executive order, or common-law doctrine to the contrary.

📦 Amendment XXXIII: Postal Delivery Accountability Amendment (PDAA) ↗

Section 1: Postal Service Guarantee

Section 1. The people shall have the right to fair, timely, secure, and reliable postal service. The United States shall maintain a national postal system that provides equal access to the collection, transportation, processing, and delivery of mail throughout the nation.

The protections and guarantees of this article shall apply equally to the national postal system and to any private or third-party entity contracted by the United States to collect, transport, process, or deliver mail and parcels. For the purposes of this article, “mail and parcels” shall encompass all tangible correspondence, goods, and physical mediums of transmission, regardless of the technology utilized for processing or transit.

Section 2: Postal Regulation and Privacy

Section 2. Congress shall have the power to establish uniform laws governing the collection, transportation, processing, tracking, and delivery of mail and parcels. Such laws shall preserve the privacy and security of sealed mail and correspondence, except as otherwise authorized by this Constitution or by law.

Section 3: Accountability for Postal Operations

Section 3. The national postal system shall maintain reasonable standards of accountability for the handling and delivery of mail. When mail or parcels are subject to unreasonable delay, loss, theft, damage, or misdelivery while in postal custody, the responsible postal authority shall investigate the matter, maintain appropriate records of custody and handling, and take reasonable measures to complete delivery or otherwise resolve the matter in accordance with law.

The postal authority shall provide an immediate, verifiable acknowledgment of physical receipt to the sender upon the transfer of any mail or parcel into its custody, the absence of which shall create a rebuttable presumption of administrative delay. Sovereign immunity is hereby waived for claims arising under this article, and remedies shall include actual and compensatory damages as prescribed by law. The United States shall provide a uniform system of postal insurance to guarantee the value of contents against loss, theft, damage, or chronic administrative delay.

Section 4: Oversight and Transparency

Section 4. Congress shall provide by law for the preservation and review of operational records, tracking information, and security measures reasonably necessary to ensure the integrity of postal operations, investigate misconduct or criminal activity, resolve customer claims, and improve the administration of the postal system. Such records and measures shall not be used to examine the contents of sealed mail except as authorized by law.

The utilization of artificial intelligence, automated algorithms, or machine learning in the sorting, routing, tracking, or management of mail and parcels shall be subject to strict human oversight and public auditability to ensure accuracy and prevent administrative misinformation.

Section 5: Extraordinary Circumstances

Section 5. Nothing in this article shall be construed to require delivery where prevented by natural disasters, armed conflict, public emergencies, threats to public safety, or other extraordinary circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the postal authority. Congress shall provide by law for procedures governing service restoration, customer notification where practicable, and appropriate remedies.

Section 6: Enforcement Clause

Section 6. Congress shall have the power to enforce, implement, and carry into execution this article by appropriate legislation, including the establishment of standards for postal operations, accountability, investigations, and remedies. Congress shall adequately appropriate funds to ensure the fulfillment of this article.

In the absence of congressional legislation defining unreasonable delay, a default standard of no more than fourteen business days for domestic delivery shall apply. Congress shall establish expedited procedures for the adjudication and payout of postal insurance and indemnity claims, which shall be resolved within thirty days of filing.

Prior to seeking judicial remedy, claimants must exhaust expedited administrative resolution procedures established by Congress, which shall be adjudicated within thirty days of filing. An administrative or algorithmic error caused by automated systems shall not alleviate the responsible postal authority of liability under this article.

💰🛡️ Amendment XXXIV: Insurance and Financial Security Amendment (IFSA) ↗

Section 1: Fundamental Right to Insurance

Section 1. The right of all persons to fair access to insurance markets, and to obtain and maintain coverage for the protection of life, health, property, income, and financial security shall not be denied, abridged, or infringed by the United States or by any State except through underwriting, exclusions, or rate-setting based on objective, actuarially justified risk factors that are not adopted or applied as a proxy for prohibited discrimination under Section 2 of this article; provided that Congress may establish general standards for implementation and enforcement of this section, which shall not be construed to define, limit, or diminish the scope of the rights guaranteed herein.

Section 2: Equal Access Clause

Section 2. No person shall be denied access to insurance on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, age, genetic information, or arbitrary algorithmic classifications; nor on any other classification that Congress may by law designate as a prohibited ground of discrimination in insurance markets, provided that such designation shall establish minimum protections that shall apply uniformly as a baseline throughout the United States and the several States, and nothing in this article shall be construed to prohibit any State from providing greater protections consistent with this article.

Section 3: Public Purpose and Financial Resilience

Section 3. Insurance infrastructure serves an essential public purpose. Congress and the several States shall possess the authority to oversee, support, and regulate insurance markets to ensure system stability, promote disaster resilience, and protect the general welfare.

Section 4: Consumer Protections Clause

Section 4. Congress and the several States may enact laws consistent with this article to ensure transparency in insurance policies, prevent fraud and deceptive practices, establish fair claims-handling standards, and provide reasonable procedures for resolving disputes between insurers and policyholders. No final determination to deny, reduce, or terminate insurance coverage or benefits shall be issued solely by automated or artificial intelligence systems, and all policyholders shall retain the right to an independent review conducted by a qualified human operator.

Section 5: Automobile Insurance Mandates

Section 5. Recognizing the importance of protecting motorists, passengers, pedestrians, and property from financial loss arising from motor vehicle accidents, Congress and the several States shall establish by law a uniform mandate of financial responsibility, verified by proof of valid insurance or approved security, as a prerequisite for the operation or registration of any motor vehicle; provided that Congress shall set minimum national baseline standards, and the States may adopt additional or more stringent requirements consistent with this article.

Such laws shall promote public safety, ensure compensation for persons injured or whose property is damaged through the operation of motor vehicles, and reduce uncompensated losses resulting from motor vehicle accidents.

Section 6: Comprehensive Insurance and Disaster Protection

Section 6. The United States and the several States may provide by law for the availability and accessibility of comprehensive insurance coverage to protect persons, families, businesses, and communities against substantial financial losses arising from natural disasters — including, but not limited to, earthquakes, hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, wildfires, landslides, volcanic eruptions, severe storms, droughts, and any other extraordinary natural, environmental, or technological events causing widespread and systemic loss, as well as declared public emergencies.

Such laws shall promote financial resilience, facilitate recovery from catastrophic losses, encourage responsible risk management, strengthen disaster preparedness, and safeguard the economic stability and general welfare of the nation.

Section 7: Essential Insurance Standards

Section 7. Congress may by law define and designate essential categories of insurance required for the protection of public health, commerce, and property, and may establish uniform baselines for their availability and continuity, provided that such classifications shall not be construed to create new constitutional entitlements beyond those expressly provided in this article.

Section 8: Fiscal Responsibility

Section 8. Nothing in this article shall be construed to require the United States to provide universal insurance coverage or unlimited public funding, nor to limit the authority of Congress to establish standards, programs, and regulations consistent with this article while preserving private insurance markets, freedom of contract, and responsible fiscal management.

Section 9: Non-Interference with Existing Rights

Section 9. Nothing in this article shall be construed to deny, diminish, or preempt any greater rights or protections related to insurance or financial security provided by federal, state, or local law; provided that such laws do not conflict with the minimum protections guaranteed under this article.

Section 10: Enforcement Clause

Section 10. Congress shall have the power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation necessary and proper to carry out the protections guaranteed herein.

⚧️⚖️ Amendment XXXV: Gender Equality Amendment (GEA) ↗

Section 1: Gender Equal Rights

Section 1. The equality of rights under the Constitution and laws of the United States shall not be denied, abridged, or infringed by the United States or by any State on account of sex or any gender‑related characteristic, including but not limited to gender identity, gender expression, transgender status, cisgender status, sexual characteristics, or any analogous classification.

Section 2: Equal Participation and Economic Opportunity

Section 2. Every person shall have an equal right to participate in all public, civic, educational, occupational, professional, athletic, recreational, governmental, commercial, and social activities, including all places of public accommodation and commercial enterprise, without discrimination on account of characteristics protected by this article.

No employer, labor organization, licensing authority, educational institution, or governmental entity shall deny employment, hiring, promotion, compensation, licensing, professional advancement, workplace benefits, educational opportunities, or economic participation on account of such characteristics. Qualifications for any occupation or opportunity must be directly related to essential functions and applied uniformly without unlawful discrimination.

Section 3: Equal Access and Nondiscrimination

Section 3. No law, regulation, policy, practice, or governmental action shall deny, exclude, segregate, or impose unequal treatment upon any person on account of characteristics protected by this article. Any classification based on such characteristics shall be subject to strict scrutiny, meaning it shall be upheld only if the government demonstrates a compelling interest and proves the measure is narrowly tailored and uses the least restrictive means available.

Section 4: Athletics and Competitive Activities

Section 4. No person shall be categorically excluded from athletics or competitive activities solely on account of characteristics protected by this article. Eligibility standards must be fair, evidence‑based, consistently applied, and nondiscriminatory, relying on demonstrable, peer‑reviewed evidence. No categorical exclusion shall be imposed without an objective, individualized assessment based on empirical, peer-reviewed scientific data, and all standards must be narrowly tailored to a compelling governmental interest using the least restrictive means available while preserving equal protection and due process.

Section 5: Privacy, Dignity, and Equal Protection

Section 5. Every person shall enjoy equal dignity, privacy, and protection under the law regardless of characteristics protected by this article. No governmental entity shall compel or indirectly compel disclosure of a person’s medical history, gender transition status, or other protected personal information except pursuant to due process of law and a compelling governmental interest.

Section 6: Construction

Section 6. Nothing in this article shall be construed to diminish or impair any right guaranteed elsewhere in this Constitution or by laws enacted pursuant thereto. This article shall be interpreted liberally and broadly to secure equal rights, equal opportunity, equal participation, and equal protection for all persons.

Section 7: Enforcement Clause

Section 7. Congress shall have the plenary power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation, including the creation of private rights of action.

States may enact protections greater than those guaranteed herein, but no State or political subdivision may enact or enforce any law that diminishes or infringes the rights secured by this article.

Section 8: Effect Delay Clause

Section 8. This article of amendment shall take effect one year after ratification. During the period preceding its effective date, the United States and the several States may enact legislation and adopt regulations necessary for implementation, provided that no such action may undermine or frustrate the purpose of this article.

💸🛑 Amendment XXXVI: Campaign Finance Integrity Amendment (CFIA) ↗

Section 1: Protection of the Rights of Natural Persons

Section 1. The rights protected by this Constitution are the rights of natural persons. Artificial entities — including corporations, limited liability companies, partnerships, labor organizations, nonprofit organizations, political committees, associations, and other entities established by law — shall have only those constitutional rights granted by the people through federal or state law, except for those procedural due process rights necessary to ensure a fair trial, protection against unlawful searches and seizures, or as explicitly granted by federal or state law. No artificial entity shall possess constitutional protections regarding the raising or spending of funds to influence elections.

Section 2: Regulation and Limitations Authority

Section 2. Congress and the States shall have the absolute authority to regulate, limit, and prohibit the raising and spending of money to influence federal, state, and local elections, including activities such as contributions, independent expenditures, coordinated expenditures, electioneering communications, ballot measure campaigns, and other expenditures intended to influence the nomination or election of candidates or the outcome of public ballot measures. Such regulation may provide for prohibiting or regulating foreign financial influence in those elections, and may be exercised to protect the integrity of the electoral process, prevent corruption and the appearance of corruption, prevent circumvention of campaign finance laws, and promote political equality.

Section 3: Disclosure Clause

Section 3.
