Congress and the States may require timely public disclosure of the true sources, beneficial owners, and amounts of funds used to influence elections, prohibit the concealment or misrepresentation of the true source of such funds, require disclosure of foreign sources of election-related funding as provided by law, and may establish systems of public financing for campaigns.

Section 4: Free Speech Clause

Section 4. Nothing in this article shall be construed to permit Congress or the States to abridge the freedom of speech or of the press, prohibit individuals from expressing political views, or discriminate against speakers or viewpoints based on the content of their expression; provided that the freedom of the press shall not be construed to immunize any artificial entity from regulations enacted pursuant to Section 2 of this article when engaging in electioneering communications. The regulation, limitation, or prohibition of financial contributions and expenditures authorized by Section 2 of this article shall be deemed fully consistent with the freedoms of speech and of the press, and shall not be construed as an abridgment thereof. Regulation authorized by this article shall be viewpoint-neutral.

Section 5: Definitions Clause

Section 5. For purposes of this article, "artificial entity" means any corporation, limited liability company, partnership, association, labor organization, political committee, nonprofit organization, or other legal entity created under the laws of the United States, any State, or any foreign jurisdiction. The terms "money," "funds," and "expenditures" shall explicitly include digital assets, cryptocurrencies, blockchain-based tokens, algorithmic systems, artificial intelligence technologies, or any other form of digital or synthetic value used to influence elections.

Section 6: Anti-Evasion Clause

Section 6. Congress and the several States shall have the authority to prohibit the circumvention or evasion of laws enacted pursuant to this article through intermediaries, affiliated entities, successor entities, coordinated activities, artificial entities, foreign persons or foreign-controlled entities, emerging technologies, decentralized networks, digital asset architectures, artificial intelligence, automated algorithmic campaigns, or any other means intended to defeat the purposes of this article.

Section 7: Enforcement Clause

Section 7. Congress shall have the power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation, and the several States shall retain concurrent authority to enact and enforce laws consistent with this article.

Section 8: Effect Delay Clause

Section 8. This article of amendment shall take effect six months after ratification. During the period preceding its effective date, the United States and the several States may enact legislation and adopt regulations necessary for implementation, provided that no such action may undermine or frustrate the purpose of this article.

These amendments are my tendency to solve 21st-century real-world issues in the United States that many people protested and expressed their frustration:

  1. Right to abortion after the Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) Supreme Court landmark decision overturned Roe v. Wade (1973) and Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992). States with total-abortion restrictions: Texas, Louisiana, Idaho.
    —
  2. Right to cellphone usage in school for students, including in cases of emergencies. States with blanket restrictions: Texas (HB 1841), Florida (HB 1105).
    —
  3. Right to strike for public-sector employees without facing severe penalties of forfeiture by the state. States with labor restrictions: Texas (Government Code § 617.003), Florida (State Statute § 447.505).
    —
  4. Democratic and electoral fairness over partisan gerrymandering in several states, as noted in Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) Supreme Court landmark decision that left with political questions beyond the reach of federal courts. Instances ahead of 2026 midterm elections in Republican-dominant states to reduce Democratic representation in Congress and state legislature, putting Democrats at a disadvantage: Texas, Tennessee, Florida.
    —
  5. Fear of deepfakes and media deception intent by improper usage of artificial intelligence (AI) media generation.
    —
  6. Postal mailing delays and information due to unexpected circumstances or informational tracking errors.
    —
  7. Importance of insurance for financial protections of people in any unexpected or extraordinary circumstances, and standard insurance mandates for vehicle drivers in regards to uninsured drivers.
    —
  8. Transgender and cisgender people limitations or denial of rights in activities, including transgender female people being restricted from participating in female-related sports and activities.
    —
  9. Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010) ruled in a 5-4 Supreme Court decision that corporate funding of independent political broadcasts cannot be limited. This established that independent political spending by corporations, labor unions, and other groups is a form of protected speech, paving the way for unlimited "independent expenditures" and the creation of Super PACs (Political Action Committees). The loophole to this includes funding in unlimited amounts, which may also be used to fund corrupt politicians or any PACs.

🏛️ Legal Authority: Precedents & Constitutional Overrides

🏥 Amendment XXVIII: Reproductive Freedom Amendment (RFA) ↗

  • Overturns: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022). By codifying reproductive freedom and bodily autonomy as a supreme constitutional right, the RFA completely strips states of the power to ban or restrict abortion care.
    —
  • Overrides: All state-level trigger laws and criminal abortion bans, including Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 170A (the Human Life Protection Act) and Texas Health & Safety Code § 171.201 (Senate Bill 8).

🎓 Amendment XXIX: Student Digital Liberty Amendment (SDLA) ↗

  • Modifies: New Jersey v. T.L.O. (1985). This landmark Supreme Court case lowered the standard for searching students in public schools from "probable cause" to mere "reasonable suspicion." The SDLA raises the bar back up, requiring a strict judicial warrant for a student's digital assets.
    —
  • Overrides: Invasive state surveillance and biometric tracking statutes, including Texas HB 1481 and Florida HB 1105, blocking districts from deploying AI surveillance, geofencing, or automated data harvesting against K-12 students.

⚙️ Amendment XXX: Labor Stoppage Amendment (LSA) ↗

  • Overturns/Modifies: The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 (29 U.S.C. § 178) and the Railway Labor Act of 1926. It strips the federal government of the power to issue sweeping, all-or-nothing injunctions to completely crush strikes or force contracts on transit and logistical unions.
    —
  • Overrides: Draconian state-level public sector strike bans, including Texas Government Code § 617.003 and Florida Statute § 447.505. This legalizes the right to strike for K-12 teachers and school staff (including in Alief ISD), public college faculty (including at University of Houston), and municipal workers, while protecting their state pensions (i.e. TRS).

🗳️ Amendment XXXI: Partisan Gerrymandering Prohibition Amendment (PGPA) ↗

  • Overturns: Rucho v. Common Cause (2019). In this 5-4 decision, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that partisan gerrymandering is a "political question" beyond the reach of the federal courts. The PGPA explicitly drags it back into the courtroom, making algorithmic map-manipulation a clear constitutional violation.
    —
  • Overrides: All state-level redistricting plans that mathematically skew electoral outcomes to favor a specific political party, completely neutralizing partisan-controlled state legislatures.

💻 Amendment XXXII: Artificial Intelligence Regulation Amendment (AIRA) ↗

  • More to be added soon.

📮 Amendment XXXIII: Postal Delivery Accountability Amendment (PDAA) ↗

  • More to be added soon.

🛡️ Amendment XXXIV: Insurance and Financial Security Amendment (IFSA) ↗

  • More to be added soon.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence Regulation Amendment (AIRA)
item.dc:creator: allenacnguyen
item.content:encoded:
I, Allen Nguyen — an independent citizen from Houston, TX, and a Summa Cum Laude graduate from the University of Houston with a Bachelor of Science in Digital Media degree — introduce a constitutional amendment that would regulate artificial intelligence, allow human sovereignty the freedom for the usage of AI (including chatbots and media generation) while implementing protections from synthetic systems, and prevent AI misusages, deceptions, fraud, human error, and harm in society.

Amendment Slogan

"Human Sovereignty over Synthetic Systems."

Baseline Philosophy

"AI does not control real humans."

Update 7/1/2026: Updated constitutional text with new sections.

Artificial Intelligence Regulation Amendment

Section 1: Purpose and Scope of Artificial Intelligence

Section 1.

1–1: Scope of Governance. Artificial intelligence (AI), including autonomous systems, generative models, robotics, and digital agents, shall be governed to protect the rights, safety, and dignity of all persons when such systems are deployed in a manner that materially affects legal rights, access to essential services, or significant personal or governmental decision-making by directly determining eligibility, approval, denial, ranking, sentencing, or materially dispositive outcomes affecting such rights or services, or by substantially influencing outcomes where a reasonable observer would conclude that the artificial intelligence system functions as a determinative or presumptively controlling factor in the decision-making process.

1–2: Functional Impact and Technological Neutrality. For purposes of this article, material effect shall be determined by the functional impact of the system on outcomes affecting legal rights, access to essential services, or governmental decision-making, rather than by the technical design or labeling of the system. Artificial intelligence usage shall be subject to constitutional safeguards that are technologically neutral and applicable to substantially equivalent computational systems regardless of architecture, methodology, or nomenclature to prevent misuse, fraudulent or deceptive conduct attributable to such systems, and harmful outcomes arising from their deployment in governmental functions or private activities materially affecting legal rights, essential services, or public welfare.

Section 2: Rights of Citizens

Section 2.

2–1: Right to Transparency. Every person shall enjoy the right to prompt and conspicuous disclosure whenever an artificial intelligence system fundamentally influences decisions determining their legal rights, liberties, or access to essential public opportunities including employment, housing, credit, education, healthcare, insurance, law enforcement action, or governmental benefits. Disclosure shall include notice of artificial intelligence involvement and the general category of decision-making influence, as defined by Congress. Such disclosure shall include, to the extent reasonably practicable and consistent with legitimate security, privacy, and proprietary interests, a plain-language explanation sufficient to permit a reasonable person to understand the principal factors materially contributing to the determination.

2–2: Requirement of Human Review. No final determination depriving a person of life, liberty, property, or fundamental rights shall be executed solely by algorithmic or automated means without independent and meaningful human review occurring prior to the final effectuation of such decision. Such review shall include independent authority to override, modify, reverse, or reject the automated determination based on a substantive review of underlying facts, evidence, and reasoning; such authority shall be final with respect to the administrative effectuation of the determination.

2–3: Standards for Meaningful Oversight. Human review shall not be satisfied by automated approval workflows, or predetermined or mechanically affirmed decisions; it shall require access to the material data inputs, outputs, documentation, and explanatory records reasonably necessary to evaluate the basis of the determination. Any human reviewer exercising authority under this Section shall possess sufficient authority, independence, and access to relevant information to conduct a meaningful and impartial evaluation of the determination. Such review shall not be satisfied by predetermined approval protocols, automated escalation filters lacking substantive discretion, or organizational structures designed to predetermine the outcome of review.

2–4: Emergency Exceptions. Congress may provide narrowly tailored emergency exceptions, applicable only to individualized determinations, where immediate action is necessary to prevent a specific, imminent, and demonstrable risk of death or serious physical injury to an identifiable person or group — provided that the invocation of such exemption is verified by a human officer, any determination executed pursuant to such emergency circumstances shall be subject to prompt post-deprivation review, and such exceptions shall not extend to generalized, statistical, or system-level risk assessments.

Section 3: Standards for AI Safety and Accountability

Section 3.

3–1: Attribution of Liability. Civil and criminal liability for actions, outputs, or damages caused by an artificial intelligence system or the autonomous physical actions of any vehicle or machinery guided thereby shall be attributed to the human or legal entity that deploys, operates, or materially controls such system in the context of its use; an autonomous system shall not be recognized as a legal person capable of bearing liability. Congress may define tiers of responsibility among developers, deployers, operators, owners, and users based upon degree of control, foreseeability, knowledge, and material contribution to the harm.

3–2: Preservation of Product Liability and Anti-Evasion. No developer, deployer, operator, owner, distributor, or materially participating entity shall evade liability through contractual delegation, indemnification agreements, corporate restructuring, or the transfer of operational control after deployment, nor shall the utilization of artificial intelligence in the design, testing, or manufacturing of a product diminish the strict product liability of its producers or distributors for defects resulting therefrom. Nothing herein shall prohibit Congress from imposing joint and several liability upon multiple responsible parties whose conduct materially contributed to the harm. Nothing in this article shall be construed to exempt governmental entities from liability, remedies, or judicial review otherwise authorized by law.

3–3: Financial Assurances and Mandatory Insurance. Congress shall possess the authority to require entities deploying autonomous or high-risk artificial intelligence systems to maintain adequate liability insurance or certified financial assurances sufficient to satisfy potential claims arising under this article.

3–4: Certification. Congress shall possess the authority to mandate rigorous safety standards and public certifications for high-risk autonomous systems defined as systems whose outputs directly affect legal rights, essential services, physical safety, or designated critical infrastructure systems designated by Congress through publicly enacted legislation and subject to periodic review deployed in commerce, government, or critical infrastructure prior to their introduction into public commerce.

Section 4: Ethical and Responsible Use

Section 4.

4–1: Prohibition of AI Misuse. The knowing utilization of artificial intelligence to perpetrate fraud, facilitate criminal impersonation, materially deceive persons in a manner causing legally cognizable harm, engage in systemic subversion of democratic processes through covert foreign state-sponsored operations or verified widespread voter deception, or facilitate the non-consensual weaponized impersonation of individuals is strictly prohibited.

4–2: Standard for Deceptive Conduct. For the purposes of this article, conduct shall be deemed deceptive when a reasonable person acting under the circumstances of distribution would foresee that the output generated by an artificial intelligence system is materially likely to mislead a reasonable person acting under similar informational conditions in the relevant medium of distribution, including political, commercial, journalistic, or private interpersonal contexts, and when the content is presented or reasonably understood under the circumstances of distribution to be human-authored or authentic human expression without adequate disclosure of artificial generation as to authorship, identity, or factual authenticity. Clearly labeled parody, satire, artistic expression, or fictional content shall not constitute deception under this Section.

4–3: Protection Against Bias. Artificial intelligence systems deployed by or on behalf of any government entity shall be designed and audited in accordance with publicly established, non-discriminatory technical standards defined by Congress or independent regulatory authority to ensure that their design, deployment, and operation do not intentionally deny or abridge equal protection under the law or produce unlawful discrimination prohibited by law. Any audit required under this article shall be conducted by an independent and professionally qualified entity possessing no direct financial interest in, ownership stake in, managerial authority over, or contractual dependency upon the system subject to audit.

4–4: Human Primacy. Artificial intelligence systems shall remain subject to identifiable human decision-making authority and ultimate human accountability whenever deployed in governmental functions or in any determination materially affecting constitutional rights, legal status, or access to essential public services. For the purposes of this Section, no artificial intelligence system shall possess independent constitutional rights, legal personhood, or authority to exercise sovereign governmental powers, except where expressly authorized by law, consistent with this Constitution, and subject at all times to meaningful human supervision and accountability, which shall remain exclusively exercised by constitutionally accountable human officers and shall not be delegated to artificial intelligence systems in whole or in part.

Section 5: Governance of Synthetic Media and Digital Likeness

Section 5.

5–1: Right to Create & Fair Use. The right of the people to generate synthetic imagery and video for lawful expressive, artistic, journalistic, and educational purposes shall not be infringed, subject to reasonable restrictions against fraud and targeted harm. This right shall not be construed to supersede the protections of Section 6 concerning voice, likeness, or personal persona. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to abridge constitutionally protected speech, including commentary, criticism, parody, satire, artistic expression, journalism, academic inquiry, or transformative works, except where such expression constitutes unlawful fraud or materially deceptive impersonation causing legally cognizable harm.

5–2: Prohibition of Deceptive Use, Disclosure, and Harm. The distribution of synthetically generated or altered visual media, including deepfake video, that depicts historical or current events with the intent to deceive the public, fabricate legal evidence, or inflict severe emotional distress through non-consensual explicit depictions is prohibited when such content is presented in a manner that creates a material risk of public deception or harm, including impersonation in political, financial, electoral, governmental, or legal contexts. Congress may require conspicuous disclosure of materially altered synthetic political communications distributed to the public during the period beginning ninety days before and ending on the date of a federal election, unless Congress prescribes a different period.

Section 6: Sovereignty of Voice and Likeness

Section 6.

6–1: Inherent Property Right. Every person possesses a protected and exclusive legal interest in their natural voice, visual likeness, and personal persona against any commercial exploitation, deceptive use, or materially misleading synthetic reproduction without explicit consent, including political advertising, endorsement, fundraising communications, and monetized digital replication, which shall extend to the person's estate for no less than a minimum period prescribed by Congress following their death; provided, however, that such right shall remain subject to limitations for matters of public concern, historical record, journalism, and constitutionally protected speech.

6–2: Prohibition of Unauthorized Replication. The unauthorized, deceptive replication or public distribution of a person’s synthetic voice or likeness is prohibited, except where such use constitutes protected commentary, parody, or news reporting, and does not create a likelihood of false endorsement or factual fabrication as determined by a reasonable consumer standard in commercial or political contexts. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to prohibit the use of a person’s likeness or voice for bona fide historical, academic, biographical, or documentary purposes; provided such use does not falsely imply endorsement or fabricate events.

6–3: Freedom of Consent. No person shall be bound by digital likeness licensing agreements lacking explicit, informed, unbundled, and revocable consent. Consent for the use of voice, likeness, or digital persona shall not be inferred from general terms-of-service agreements or bundled contracts — it must be obtained through clear, separate, and affirmative authorization; provided, that Congress may define standardized consent frameworks for limited commercial licensing agreements.

6–4: Protection of Data and Identity. Congress shall have the authority to establish reasonable safeguards governing the collection, retention, use, and commercial exploitation of personal data by artificial intelligence systems where necessary to protect privacy, identity, property, or individual autonomy consistent with this Constitution. Such safeguards shall be narrowly tailored to legitimate privacy and identity-protection interests and shall not be construed to prohibit lawful scientific research, security testing, or public-interest data analysis conducted in accordance with applicable law.

Section 7: Governance and Oversight

Section 7.

7–1: Regulatory Framework and Suspension Power. Congress shall provide for independent oversight of advanced artificial intelligence systems through such authority, agency, commission, or regulatory framework as it may establish by law. Such authority shall possess the power to temporarily suspend or isolate specific components of systems presenting a clear, demonstrable, imminent, and catastrophic threat to public safety, national security, or constitutional order via the most narrowly tailored means available where less restrictive regulatory measures are insufficient to mitigate such threat.

7–2: Evidentiary Standards and Judicial Review. No suspension shall issue absent documented findings supported by clear and convincing evidence. Such findings shall be subject to prompt judicial review, and the evidentiary standard shall be evaluated de novo by the reviewing court. For the purposes of this article, a “clear, demonstrable, imminent, and catastrophic threat” shall mean a demonstrable and immediate risk of mass casualty, catastrophic infrastructure failure, or large-scale disruption of democratic governance. Congress shall receive prompt notice of any suspension issued under this Section and may prescribe additional procedures for oversight and review.

7–3: Due Process and Judicial Review. No suspension under this Section shall be used to override or nullify individual due process rights guaranteed under Section 2 — except where such suspension is itself necessary to prevent imminent catastrophic harm as defined herein. Any suspension shall be subject to prompt judicial review within a period prescribed by Congress, which shall not unreasonably delay judicial consideration of the suspension.

7–4: Limitations and Institutional Integrity. No suspension under this Section shall exceed the minimum duration necessary to mitigate the identified threat; it shall automatically terminate upon cessation of such threat unless renewed by a separate judicial determination. The governing structure of such authority shall provide institutional independence, transparency, public reporting, and protections against direct partisan control as defined by Congress.

Section 8: Sovereignty and Security of AI Infrastructure

Section 8.

8–1: Infrastructure Classification and Grid Resilience. Advanced artificial intelligence data centers, hyperscale computing facilities, and the primary physical infrastructure underpinning high-risk automated systems are recognized as strategic national utilities vital to public infrastructure and national security. No human or legal entity shall construct, expand, or operate such facilities in a manner that compromises the stability, reliability, or baseline capacity of local or national electrical grids, nor shall the energy demands of such facilities disproportionately shift utility costs onto residential consumers.

8–2: Environmental and Resource Guardrails. The operation of advanced computing infrastructure shall remain subject to strict public accountability regarding natural resource consumption. Congress and the several States shall retain the authority to regulate, limit, or condition the extraction of public water resources and the utilization of fossil-fuel power generation by data center facilities to prevent localized ecological degradation, systemic environmental harm, or the subversion of state and local resource management.

8–3: Physical Security and Sovereign Continuity. As critical infrastructure, hyperscale data centers hosting advanced artificial intelligence systems shall be hardened against physical, kinetic, and digital threats to ensure sovereign operational continuity. The ownership, material control, or structural leasing of critical computing infrastructure within the United States by prohibited foreign adversaries or their proxies is strictly prohibited.

Section 9: Innovation and Public Benefit

Section 9. Congress and the States shall possess the authority to incentivize and promote the development of artificial intelligence systems designed to advance the public welfare and common defense. Safety standards and best practices shall be publicly accessible. This article shall be construed in a technologically neutral manner and shall apply to future computational systems performing substantially equivalent functions to those regulated herein. Nothing in this article shall be construed to prohibit lawful scientific research, open scientific publication, security research, testing, or academic inquiry conducted in accordance with applicable law.

Section 10: Definitions

Section 10.

10–1: Definition of Artificial Intelligence. ‘Artificial intelligence’ refers to computational systems that generate predictions, classifications, recommendations, decisions, or content through machine-learned, adaptive, inferential, probabilistic, or substantially equivalent computational processes, including systems that functionally replicate such capabilities regardless of underlying architecture, methodology, or implementation.

10–2: Definition of AI-Generated Imagery and Video. ‘AI‑generated imagery and video’ includes photorealistic, synthetic, or materially altered visual content, moving images, or cinematographic sequences produced or modified by artificial intelligence, including depictions that a reasonable observer could mistake for authentic recordings.

10–3: Definition of Deepfake Video. ‘Deepfake video’ refers to synthetically generated or altered digital video recordings that realistically depict a person’s likeness, actions, or speech occurring in a manner that did not actually transpire, produced with the intent or effect of appearing authentic to a reasonable observer.

10–4: Definition of AI-Generated Voice. ‘AI-generated voice’ refers to synthetic audio replicating or imitating a natural human voice.

10–5: Definition of Likeness. ‘Likeness’ includes the unique visual, auditory, or behavioral characteristics identifying a specific individual.

10–6: Definition of Autonomous System. ‘Autonomous system’ refers to any machine, software, or computational process capable of operating without continuous human direction in a manner that materially affects human rights, property, or public infrastructure.

10–7: Definition of Digital Persona. ‘Digital persona’ refers to the composite of a person’s identifiable characteristics, including voice, likeness, mannerisms, behavioral patterns, or other attributes that enable recognition in digital or synthetic media when such use is intended to represent a specific identifiable individual.

Section 11: Anti-Evasion Clause

Section 11. Neither the United States nor any State, nor any public or private actor subject to this article, shall evade the protections or restrictions herein through contractual arrangements, technological intermediaries, nominal human oversight, corporate restructuring, geographic displacement, or through any substantially equivalent mechanism, arrangement, designation, intermediary, or technological process whose practical effect is to circumvent the protections or obligations established by this article, whether formally designated as artificial intelligence or described by any other technological classification. The protections and obligations of this article shall not be avoided through foreign outsourcing, intermediary entities, subcontracting arrangements, or materially equivalent operational structures.

Section 12: Severability Clause

Section 12. If any provision of this article, or the application thereof, is held invalid, the remainder of the article and its application to other persons or circumstances shall remain in full force and effect to the maximum extent constitutionally permissible.

Section 13: Enforcement Clause

Section 13.

13–1: Legislative Enforcement Power. Congress shall have the power to enforce and implement this article by appropriate legislation, including civil penalties, administrative enforcement mechanisms, and judicially reviewable regulatory standards consistent with this article.

13–2: Due Process Balance. In the event of conflict between emergency suspension powers under Section 7 and individual rights under Section 2, courts shall apply the least restrictive interpretation necessary to preserve constitutional due process consistent with imminent catastrophic risk prevention.

13–3: Standing and Equitable Remedies. Any person suffering a concrete, particularized, or legally cognizable injury arising from a violation of this article shall have standing to seek injunctive relief, declaratory relief, and damages where authorized by law, upon showing that the artificial intelligence system or its deployment was a substantial and proximate factor in the injury, without requirement of showing exclusive causation, and shall be entitled to such additional equitable relief as necessary to fully remedy the violation.

Section 14: Immediate Effect Clause

Section 14. This article of amendment shall take effect immediately upon ratification by three-fourths of the States. This article shall be entirely self-executing, immediately operative upon ratification, and judicially enforceable without the prerequisite of enabling legislation; and the absence of congressional enforcement legislation shall not be construed to delay, restrict, or deny the immediate judicial enforcement of any right guaranteed herein; notwithstanding any prior statute, executive order, or common-law doctrine to the contrary.

📊 The AIRA Portfolio Evaluation Matrix

The reason why I introduce this constitutional amendment

As advanced technology, including artificial intelligence, evolves in the 21st century, I believe artificial intelligence should be regulated for human sovereignty over synthetic systems, and prevent AI misusage, deceptions, fraud, human error, and harm in society. My philosophical line when I think about the amendment idea that should regulate AI and protect humans:

"AI does not control real humans."

The purpose of the Artificial Intelligence Regulation Amendment (AIRA) is to future-proof artificial intelligence with regulations for human sovereignty and protections. Any physical robots, computer systems, or vehicles that are controlled by itself must be human-directed to prevent misusage and harm. I also mentioned about AI data centers, which is a loophole that needs to be addressed.

In this constitutional amendment, I choose not to include the sunset clause, which would give states in the nation a limited amount of time to ratify passed amendments. So, by excluding the sunset clause, I choose to give states flexibility upon passage by Congress on legislative discussions to ratify this constitutional amendment on preventing any gerrymandered maps in the future.

Constitutional amendments require broad public support and careful national debate. While the Artificial Intelligence Regulation Amendment (AIRA) may be controversial, I welcome constructive comments, criticism, and proposed changes from the public as part of the constitutional process. This is one of the most complex constitutional amendments to draft to future-proof artificial intelligence and protect people as advanced technology evolves.

Steps to take this amendment into law

Once I finalize the draft of this constitutional amendment with some help from other people, legal scholars, or lawmakers by means of review and evaluation, then I would send this amendment article to Washington, D.C., at the U.S. Capitol Hill for Congress to attempt to pass this amendment.

First, under Article V of the United States Constitution in terms of getting the amendment into law, Congress must vote 2/3 in both the House of Representatives and the Senate to pass this constitutional amendment.

  • 290 out of 435 House of Representatives are required to pass
  • 67 out of 100 Senators are required to pass

Alternatively, under Article V of the United States Constitution, a national convention can be called on proposing this constitutional amendment if 2/3 (34 out of 50 states) of state legislatures apply to Congress to do so. This method was never utilized in U.S. history.

Once this constitutional amendment is passed by Congress, then the next step is ratification, which requires at least 3/4 of the states to ratify this constitutional amendment.

  • 38 out of 50 States are required to ratify

If this Artificial Intelligence Regulation Amendment (AIRA) is ratified into the United States Constitution, then it would become the 28th Amendment to the United States Constitution (or 29th Amendment if the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) is officially ratified and certified first that it was in legal limbo for decades since expiration). This constitutional amendment would future-proof artificial intelligence as modern and advanced technology evolves.

Sponsorship List

item.title: Postal Delivery Accountability Amendment (PDAA)
item.dc:creator: allenacnguyen
item.content:encoded:
I, Allen Nguyen — an independent citizen from Houston, TX, and a Summa Cum Laude graduate from the University of Houston with a Bachelor of Science in Digital Media degree — introduce a constitutional amendment that tends to resolve postal mailing delivery delay and misinformation issues, ensuring on-time deliveries.

Amendment Slogan

"Reliable Mail. Accountable Service."

Update 7/6/2026: Updated body font.

Postal Delivery Accountability Amendment

Section 1: Postal Service Guarantee

Section 1. The people shall have the right to fair, timely, secure, and reliable postal service. The United States shall maintain a national postal system that provides equal access to the collection, transportation, processing, and delivery of mail throughout the nation.

The protections and guarantees of this article shall apply equally to the national postal system and to any private or third-party entity contracted by the United States to collect, transport, process, or deliver mail and parcels. For the purposes of this article, “mail and parcels” shall encompass all tangible correspondence, goods, and physical mediums of transmission, regardless of the technology utilized for processing or transit.

Section 2: Postal Regulation and Privacy

Section 2. Congress shall have the power to establish uniform laws governing the collection, transportation, processing, tracking, and delivery of mail and parcels. Such laws shall preserve the privacy and security of sealed mail and correspondence, except as otherwise authorized by this Constitution or by law.

Section 3: Accountability for Postal Operations

Section 3. The national postal system shall maintain reasonable standards of accountability for the handling and delivery of mail. When mail or parcels are subject to unreasonable delay, loss, theft, damage, or misdelivery while in postal custody, the responsible postal authority shall investigate the matter, maintain appropriate records of custody and handling, and take reasonable measures to complete delivery or otherwise resolve the matter in accordance with law.

The postal authority shall provide an immediate, verifiable acknowledgment of physical receipt to the sender upon the transfer of any mail or parcel into its custody, the absence of which shall create a rebuttable presumption of administrative delay. Sovereign immunity is hereby waived for claims arising under this article, and remedies shall include actual and compensatory damages as prescribed by law. The United States shall provide a uniform system of postal insurance to guarantee the value of contents against loss, theft, damage, or chronic administrative delay.

Section 4: Oversight and Transparency

Section 4. Congress shall provide by law for the preservation and review of operational records, tracking information, and security measures reasonably necessary to ensure the integrity of postal operations, investigate misconduct or criminal activity, resolve customer claims, and improve the administration of the postal system. Such records and measures shall not be used to examine the contents of sealed mail except as authorized by law.

The utilization of artificial intelligence, automated algorithms, or machine learning in the sorting, routing, tracking, or management of mail and parcels shall be subject to strict human oversight and public auditability to ensure accuracy and prevent administrative misinformation.

Section 5: Extraordinary Circumstances

Section 5. Nothing in this article shall be construed to require delivery where prevented by natural disasters, armed conflict, public emergencies, threats to public safety, or other extraordinary circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the postal authority. Congress shall provide by law for procedures governing service restoration, customer notification where practicable, and appropriate remedies.

Section 6: Enforcement Clause

Section 6. Congress shall have the power to enforce, implement, and carry into execution this article by appropriate legislation, including the establishment of standards for postal operations, accountability, investigations, and remedies. Congress shall adequately appropriate funds to ensure the fulfillment of this article.

In the absence of congressional legislation defining unreasonable delay, a default standard of no more than fourteen business days for domestic delivery shall apply. Congress shall establish expedited procedures for the adjudication and payout of postal insurance and indemnity claims, which shall be resolved within thirty days of filing.

Prior to seeking judicial remedy, claimants must exhaust expedited administrative resolution procedures established by Congress, which shall be adjudicated within thirty days of filing. An administrative or algorithmic error caused by automated systems shall not alleviate the responsible postal authority of liability under this article.

📊 The PDAA Portfolio Evaluation Matrix

The reason why I introduce this constitutional amendment

I believe postal mailing delays and misinformation should be accounted for, and ensure accuracy and efficiency of on-time deliveries.

The purpose of the Postal Delivery Accountability Amendment (PDAA) is to account for postal services with accuracy to prevent delays and misinformation for on-time deliveries of physical mails and packages to intended addresses.

In this constitutional amendment, I choose not to include the sunset clause, which would give states in the nation a limited amount of time to ratify passed amendments. So, by excluding the sunset clause, I choose to give states flexibility upon passage by Congress on legislative discussions to ratify this constitutional amendment on preventing any gerrymandered maps in the future.

Constitutional amendments require broad public support and careful national debate. While the Postal Delivery Accountability Amendment (PDAA) may be controversial, I welcome constructive comments, criticism, and proposed changes from the public as part of the constitutional process. This is the amendment that I've been thinking about accounting postal delays and misinformation, and ensuring accuracy and efficiency in on-time postal mailing deliveries to intended destinations.

Steps to take this amendment into law

Once I finalize the draft of this constitutional amendment with some help from other people, legal scholars, or lawmakers by means of review and evaluation, then I would send this amendment article to Washington, D.C., at the U.S. Capitol Hill for Congress to attempt to pass this amendment.

First, under Article V of the United States Constitution in terms of getting the amendment into law, Congress must vote 2/3 in both the House of Representatives and the Senate to pass this constitutional amendment.

  • 290 out of 435 House of Representatives are required to pass
  • 67 out of 100 Senators are required to pass

Alternatively, under Article V of the United States Constitution, a national convention can be called on proposing this constitutional amendment if 2/3 (34 out of 50 states) of state legislatures apply to Congress to do so. This method was never utilized in U.S. history.

Once this constitutional amendment is passed by Congress, then the next step is ratification, which requires at least 3/4 of the states to ratify this constitutional amendment.

  • 38 out of 50 States are required to ratify

If this Postal Delivery Accountability Amendment (PDAA) is ratified into the United States Constitution, then it would become the 28th Amendment to the United States Constitution (or 29th Amendment if the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) is officially ratified and certified first that it was in legal limbo for decades since expiration). This constitutional amendment would account on delays and misinformation on postal deliveries, and ensure on-time deliveries.

item.title: Insurance and Financial Security Amendment (IFSA)
item.dc:creator: allenacnguyen
item.content:encoded:
I, Allen Nguyen — an independent citizen from Houston, TX, and a Summa Cum Laude graduate from the University of Houston with a Bachelor of Science in Digital Media degree — introduce a constitutional amendment that explicitly mentions the importance of insurance to protect people from financial loss in unexpected circumstances, and the mandatory regulation of auto insurance for vehicle drivers in the event of vehicle accidents.

Amendment Slogan

"Protected Against Risk. Secured for Recovery."

Update 6/30/2026: Created IFSA article.

Insurance and Financial Security Amendment

Section 1: Fundamental Right to Insurance

Section 1. The right of all persons to fair access to insurance markets, and to obtain and maintain coverage for the protection of life, health, property, income, and financial security shall not be denied, abridged, or infringed by the United States or by any State except through underwriting, exclusions, or rate-setting based on objective, actuarially justified risk factors that are not adopted or applied as a proxy for prohibited discrimination under Section 2 of this article; provided that Congress may establish general standards for implementation and enforcement of this section, which shall not be construed to define, limit, or diminish the scope of the rights guaranteed herein.

Section 2: Equal Access Clause

Section 2. No person shall be denied access to insurance on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, age, genetic information, or arbitrary algorithmic classifications; nor on any other classification that Congress may by law designate as a prohibited ground of discrimination in insurance markets, provided that such designation shall establish minimum protections that shall apply uniformly as a baseline throughout the United States and the several States, and nothing in this article shall be construed to prohibit any State from providing greater protections consistent with this article.

Section 3: Public Purpose and Financial Resilience

Section 3. Insurance infrastructure serves an essential public purpose. Congress and the several States shall possess the authority to oversee, support, and regulate insurance markets to ensure system stability, promote disaster resilience, and protect the general welfare.

Section 4: Consumer Protections Clause

Section 4. Congress and the several States may enact laws consistent with this article to ensure transparency in insurance policies, prevent fraud and deceptive practices, establish fair claims-handling standards, and provide reasonable procedures for resolving disputes between insurers and policyholders. No final determination to deny, reduce, or terminate insurance coverage or benefits shall be issued solely by automated or artificial intelligence systems, and all policyholders shall retain the right to an independent review conducted by a qualified human operator.

Section 5: Automobile Insurance Mandates

Section 5. Recognizing the importance of protecting motorists, passengers, pedestrians, and property from financial loss arising from motor vehicle accidents, Congress and the several States shall establish by law a uniform mandate of financial responsibility, verified by proof of valid insurance or approved security, as a prerequisite for the operation or registration of any motor vehicle; provided that Congress shall set minimum national baseline standards, and the States may adopt additional or more stringent requirements consistent with this article.

Such laws shall promote public safety, ensure compensation for persons injured or whose property is damaged through the operation of motor vehicles, and reduce uncompensated losses resulting from motor vehicle accidents.

Section 6: Comprehensive Insurance and Disaster Protection

Section 6. The United States and the several States may provide by law for the availability and accessibility of comprehensive insurance coverage to protect persons, families, businesses, and communities against substantial financial losses arising from natural disasters — including, but not limited to, earthquakes, hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, wildfires, landslides, volcanic eruptions, severe storms, droughts, and any other extraordinary natural, environmental, or technological events causing widespread and systemic loss, as well as declared public emergencies.

Such laws shall promote financial resilience, facilitate recovery from catastrophic losses, encourage responsible risk management, strengthen disaster preparedness, and safeguard the economic stability and general welfare of the nation.

Section 7: Essential Insurance Standards

Section 7. Congress may by law define and designate essential categories of insurance required for the protection of public health, commerce, and property, and may establish uniform baselines for their availability and continuity, provided that such classifications shall not be construed to create new constitutional entitlements beyond those expressly provided in this article.

Section 8: Fiscal Responsibility

Section 8. Nothing in this article shall be construed to require the United States to provide universal insurance coverage or unlimited public funding, nor to limit the authority of Congress to establish standards, programs, and regulations consistent with this article while preserving private insurance markets, freedom of contract, and responsible fiscal management.

Section 9: Non-Interference with Existing Rights

Section 9. Nothing in this article shall be construed to deny, diminish, or preempt any greater rights or protections related to insurance or financial security provided by federal, state, or local law; provided that such laws do not conflict with the minimum protections guaranteed under this article.

Section 10: Enforcement Clause

Section 10. Congress shall have the power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation necessary and proper to carry out the protections guaranteed herein.
